#4841. Building Community Takes More Than an Invitation

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 1, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

I’ve been reading The Middle of Somewhere: Rural Education Partnerships and Innovation, edited by Hartman and Klein, a book about rural school communities and partnerships. As I read, I keep thinking about the energy it takes to build a community. It involves learning what matters to people, finding ways to contribute, and being willing to receive what others offer. Those ideas stayed with me while watching Hallmark’s Who’s Coming for Christmas? The main character's wish to fill her Christmas table raises a question that extends well beyond the holidays: How do we create a community when we are still trying to find our place in it?

Julie just moved to Pine Tree Lane. She is learning a new job as the head librarian, getting to know her neighbors, and imagining what her life might become. After meeting a neighbor, who is a divorced father, and his daughter, a voracious reader who also writes poetry, she explains her dream of having a full table for Christmas.

Two of the dining room table seats were to be held for Julie’s parents, but they won a Christmas cruise. Facing an empty table in a town where she’s starting over, she begins to doubt that she’ll have anyone at her table for Christmas. She must decide to build her community by meeting new people who will fill her table or put aside her dream until next year and dine alone. Mark agrees to introduce her to community members, sold on her optimism about meeting eight people to fill her Christmas table.

Julie’s dining room table represents more than a place to eat. It represents something many of us want when we move or experience a major transition: people with whom to share our lives. We may know where to buy groceries, get a haircut, and how to get to work long before we know whom to invite over or call when we need company. Julie approaches that uncertainty with optimism and vulnerability. She needs to both let people know that she wants to spend time with them and hope that they would like that, too.

The Social Identity Model of Identity Change offers a way to understand what both Julie and Mark are building. This model suggests that maintaining meaningful group connections and developing new ones can help us adjust during life transitions. Julie’s grandmother’s table symbolizes continuity with her family, while her invitations create opportunities to become part of a new community. Mark is maintaining his connection with Vanessa while exploring how their holiday traditions and local relationships can grow following his divorce. Viewed through this lens, both characters are finding ways to carry meaningful parts of their lives into a future that includes new sources of belonging.

Julie is also building community through her work at the library, especially among young readers. Books offer a starting point for connection. A shared interest can open a conversation, and returning to a welcoming space can give people opportunities to become familiar with one another.

Mark’s daughter, Vanessa, loves reading and writing. Her interests offer a way for Julie to connect with her as a person with ideas and stories worth hearing. That attention matters. Creating community involves learning who people are and making room for what they bring. In fact, Vanessa is the first to share her poetry at the Christmas Voices event Julie organizes to increase interest at the library.

Building community also involves receiving. We may find it comfortable to offer help, organize an event, or invite someone to dinner. Accepting help can feel more exposing. It means acknowledging that we have needs, sharing those needs with others, and allowing someone else to see those needs and respond. Whether we’re new to a community or building a new community of friends, this can be challenging. For Julie, building community means allowing other people to help shape the life she is creating.

Julie begins to believe that her table will be full in time for Christmas and can’t help but feel disappointed as people begin cancelling. An invitation can seem like a simple gesture until we wait for an answer or see those plans unravel. All of a sudden, a simple invitation becomes much bigger than spending an evening together.

For someone establishing new relationships, a cancellation may have us asking uncomfortable questions. Did I misunderstand our connection? Was I too eager? Do I matter to these people? Those feelings can arise even when the cancellation has a reasonable explanation. In Julie’s case, weather disrupts plans. Disappointment is real, but it does not necessarily tell us how much others care.

Nurturing community requires willingness to remain open through this uncertainty. That does not mean repeatedly pursuing people who show no interest. It means leaving room for relationships to develop without asking each interaction to prove that we belong.

Hallmark: A Christmas table offers a visible, satisfying picture of people coming together.

Psychology: The relationships around that table depend on what happens beyond the celebration: paying attention, following through, accepting help, and reaching out again.

The Verdict: Hallmark is on the right track but misses the full range of community building. A full table is one possible expression of community. A smaller gathering can hold meaningful connection, too.

The book I’m reading has prompted me to think about how much participation community asks of us. Julie and Mark remind me that this includes the willingness to be new, to need people, and to make an invitation without knowing exactly how it will be received.

#4840. Bijan Robinson Has a Secret Weapon. It’s Not What You Think.

The Falcons star approaches this area of health with the same discipline as his game.

BIJAN ROBINSON DOESN’T lack confidence. The Atlanta Falcons running back has been one of the best players at his position even before his days in the NFL, when he was a top back at the University of Texas and a number one-rated recruit going into college. He’s not afraid to show it, either. “If you know me, [you know] I smile a lot,” he tells Men’s Health.

As much as he has depended on his smile to project his self-assurance, Robinson didn’t always feel the best about his teeth. He recalls some slightly awkward stages in his younger years. “When I was a kid, more middle school, I was still kind of growing into my teeth,” he says. “I had two teeth that would kind of twist in a little bit.”

For lots of guys, the state of their smile is a huge concern. But Robinson didn’t want to go through the trouble of getting braces to address the issue. “I was still trying to avoid having a wire on my teeth, because I thought that it would limit me from eating certain things, trying to keep it straight.” Robinson grew into his smile, and didn’t worry as much about his teeth as he became one of the most celebrated football players in the country.

But when he eventually entered the NFL, he realized how a small fix could make a big difference for his professional image. Robinson partnered with Invisalign and began wearing the clear aligners to straighten out that little twist in his smile.

“You're in front of a camera a lot in interviews and even just talking to people [at] events,” he says. “Having [my] smile is not only a confidence booster for myself, but the other I'm talking to—it makes them more engaged in the conversation. They see you take care of yourself.”

Robinson says he wears the aligners everywhere—even with his helmet on in practice and in games. He says a traditional mouthguard makes it difficult for him to breathe, and his conditioning is what gives him an edge as a back who can score out of the backfield as a runner and receiver. (Invisalign reps clarified it should not be used as a mouthguard).

Overall, Robinson appreciates how he’s able to make his oral health another aspect of the self-discipline and self-improvement practices that have helped him to be such a standout player. Like his workouts and skill-position drills, he takes it seriously. His smile is also his responsibility. “I'm not only representing myself,” he says. “I'm representing the Falcons, my family—everybody.”

Brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

#4838. Cutting Back on Ultra-Processed Foods May Help Ease Depression Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emerging research has linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) with an increased risk of depression. Now, a small study published September 23 in JAMA Psychiatrysuggests that reducing UPF intake may help ease depression symptoms.

There is no universally accepted definition of UPFs. However, a widely used classification system known as NOVA defines them as industrial formulations made primarily from substances extracted or derived from foods, often with additives not typically used in home cooking. Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, candy, sausages, hot dogs, and pastries.

Previous research has linked UPFs to an increased risk of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and other mental health conditions. In the new study, participants reduced their UPF intake by more than 85% and had significantly lower depression scores across three standard measures while following the low-UPF diet.

This small study included 20 participants who:

The participants also had to agree not to change medications, therapy, exercise, or sleep during the study.

Of the 20 participants enrolled in the study, 19 completed it. The average age was 44. Participants followed both their usual diet and a low-UPF diet during separate phases of the study, with the order randomly assigned.

Participants generally found the low-UPF diet acceptable and manageable. They also had lower depression and anxiety scores during the low-UPF diet phase compared with their usual diet.

On one commonly used depression measure, the PHQ-9, average scores declined from 8.68 during the usual diet phase to 5.53 during the low-UPF phase.

The study had several limitations, including its small sample size, reliance on self-reported dietary data, and uncertainty about which aspects of reducing UPFs may have contributed to the changes in symptoms.

The researchers also said that larger studies are needed to determine whether reducing UPF intake can improve depression symptoms.

Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study, agreed, noting that more research is needed to understand whether reducing UPFs directly improves depression symptoms or whether other aspects of the overall diet may be contributing to the observed benefit.

Dara Houp, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist with Pathways Psychological Services in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it’s important to distinguish ultra-processed foods from processed foods more broadly.

Routhenstein agreed that the distinction is important. “Processing is not inherently negative. Many nutritious foods are processed in some way.”

“I would not encourage people to simply label a food as ‘processed’ or ‘unprocessed’ and make decisions based on that label alone. I prefer to look at the overall dietary pattern, the nutritional value of the food, and what role that food plays in the diet. A packaged food can still provide meaningful nutrients and be part of an overall nutritious eating pattern,” she said.

There are various proposed mechanisms for how UPFs may affect mood.

For example, UPFs are often low in fiber, vitamins, and minerals, which can play important roles in brain health.

Houp noted that some ingredients found in UPFs, including artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, may affect the gut microbiome.

“Our gut is a primary location for producing neurotransmitters, responsible for manufacturing the vast majority – upward of 90% – of our body’s serotonin. When the gut microbiome is disrupted, it directly interferes with healthy neurotransmitter production,” she said.

Houp added that diets high in UPFs may be lower in antioxidant-rich foods, such as fruits and vegetables, which could contribute to oxidative stress. Research suggests that people with depression may have lower antioxidant levels and higher markers of oxidative damage.

Routhenstein also noted that researchers are investigating how UPF consumption may influence inflammation, metabolic health, and the gut-brain axis, all of which may have implications for mood.

Reducing your UPF intake can start with small, sustainable changes.

Routhenstein suggested starting by looking at the foods you eat most often rather than trying to overhaul your kitchen.

“Identify one or two foods that are frequent sources of UPFs and consider what you could realistically replace them with. For example, you might swap a daily sugary drink for water or sparkling water, or choose fruit, nuts, yogurt, or another minimally processed option in place of a packaged snack,” she said.

Other ways you can help reduce UPFs include:

Routhenstein added that you don’t have to eliminate convenience from your diet. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, canned fish, oats, plain yogurt, tofu, and other minimally processed foods can make healthy eating much more practical.

“The goal is not to eat a perfectly unprocessed diet. It is to gradually shift the overall pattern toward more nutrient-dense foods that provide fiber, protein, healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals,” she said.

#4837. The Men's Health Ultimate Guide to Peptides

A science-backed guide to understanding the use, side effects, and supporting research behind the emerging substances.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AS THE CURIOSITY around peptides grows, the FDA has made efforts in removing a portion of the 19 synthetic peptides from the Category 2 Bulk Substances List. This is kind of a huge deal because when the FDA classifies a substance as Category 2 they believe that it carries significant safety risks, and prohibit compounding pharmacies from making it.

In July 2026, an FDA advisory committee met to evaluate evidence for seven popular synthetic peptides on the Category 2 list and recommend whether the FDA should move them onto the Category 1 list, which allows them to be made. Another five will be under review in 2027.The FDA is not bound to the advisory committee’s recommendations.

The panel voted to loosen the restrictions on BPC-157 and TB-500 (those make up the infamous “Wolverine Stack”), as well as KPV, MOTS-C, Epitalon and Semax. It voted no for Emedeltide; that’s the one people reach for to help their sleep. None of the compounds scored a unanimous vote. This October, US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. pushed forward a policy to temporarily increase access to these six unapproved peptides. The government will not penalize licensed pharmacists in compounding pharmacies for creating and distributing these substances for people with a prescription. The nudge from RFK Jr. to allow the temporary sale of peptides has received mixed reactions.

”The American Peptide Association applauds the efforts of the Trump Administration and HHS to green light certain peptides into production by compound pharmacies,” Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association wrote in an email to MH. “It is much needed clarity that the peptide industry, clinicians and consumers have hoped and worked for for the past couple years and is a bold step outside the usual pharma driven, FDA managed pathway.”

Motisola Lewis, MD, is an internal medicine physician who runs her own concierge medical practice working to fix a broken medical system. While she focuses on providing personalized care to her patients, she doesn’t agree with expanding access to unapproved peptides before having adequate evidence of their safety and effectiveness. “I want patients to have access to promising treatments, but I also want those treatments to be supported by good science. My concern is that the enthusiasm around peptides has moved much faster than the clinical evidence.” For Dr. Lewis, several questions are still missing that the FDA has not answered: do these peptides actually work and for whom, peptide quality especially from third-party suppliers, and who is in charge of oversight. That doesn’t mean she is unwilling to discuss peptides, which is happening more than ever.

Sritha Rajupet, MD, MPH, chair of the department of family, population, and preventive medicine at Stony Brook Medicine, also has concerns. “Most of these peptides still lack high-quality human data on safety, effectiveness, and appropriate dosing,” Dr. Rajupet says. Meaning that even if the FDA removes the Category 2 label, there’s still not a lot of research around if and how they work—along with any side effects. In the document outlining RFK Jr’s new policy, compounding pharmacists must report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded.”

Still, Dr. Rajupet acknowledges that people are interested in synthetic peptides—and many are already obtaining them through unregulated channels.

Kent Bradley, MD, sees this at his role of chief medical officer at 10X Health, which offers synthetic peptide therapy. “Many of the people reaching for peptides have already exhausted conventional options,” he says. “The issue we are seeing is that individuals may have gotten a peptide without going through legitimate quality checks of a compounded pharmacy and self-administering based on information they are seeing off of social media.”

The world of synthetic peptides is promising, for sure. But there are dangers—some of which are serious (ahem, cancer). Dr. Rajupet says that in order for consumers to protect themselves, they have to study up.

“From a clinical perspective, the priority is balancing harm reduction with scientific rigor—engaging patients in open, nonjudgmental conversations while being clear that many of these therapies remain experimental, with uncertain risks and benefits,” says Dr. Rajupet.

For this reason, we created a one-stop glossary to help answer your questions about the current peptide-palooza we’re in now. Here’s the hype—and actual science.

WELL, KNOW THAT peptides exist naturally. Technically, they’re short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of protein. And not just the kind of protein that builds biceps. Proteins can also act as messengers throughout your body, doing everything from signaling the release a particular hormone to regulating inflammatory responses.

But when we’re talking about the kind of peptides the FDA will consider for deregulation, we’re talking about synthetic peptides delivered through sprays or injection. These drugs work to trigger the same responses as natural peptides, but the science is in its very early stages. Anecdotal evidence from who take peptides have reported improvements in their health, appearance, and muscle performance. But, again, anecdotal.

These are the synthetic peptides that the FDA will consider for deregulation in 2026 and 2027, broken into categories based on their supposed health benefits. And we gave each a thumbs up, thumbs down, or thumbs "meh" to rate just how much the science backs up the supposed benefits.

Known as the fat burning peptide, AOD-9604 mimics human growth hormone to promote lipolysis, or the breakdown of stored fat. Scientists are using the peptide as a possible treatment for obesity and people are taking the peptide recreationally to burn body fat, boost fat metabolism, and support body recomposition. There is also discussion of AOD-9604 helping with joint pain, mobility, and collagen production. One of the supposed benefits of AOD-9604 is that it sheds fat without affecting blood sugar or inducing insulin resistance.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: The studies on the effectiveness and safety of AOD-9604 go back roughly a decade. The research was largely conducted on animals and most of the studies that showed positive results were funded or led by researchers from the pharmaceutical company that developed AOD-9604.

This peptide reportedly protects the cell by providing more “fuel” for increased stamina. So people who report fatigue are taking the peptide to improve energy and metabolism. Because MOTS-C is supposed to target mitochondria, the energy sources of a cell, you’ll see it promoted in longevity stacks.RESEARCH SUMMARY: While there has been extensive research into the physiological function of MOTS-C, there is a lack of clinical trial data testing the safety and effectiveness of the peptide.

Semax is considered a brain-boosting peptide often given as a nasal spray. Anecdotal reports detail improvements in memory, attention, and deeper mental awareness. Semax is supposed to work by raising a protein called brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) that is important for learning and strengthening connection between brain cells.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Most of the research in Semax that claims it has neuroprotective effects come from Russia, where the peptide is used in the treatment of people with stroke. The Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation reviewed the Russian pilot studies in humans and found a lack of strong evidence demonstrating that Semax would improve cognition in healthy individuals or in the prevention of cognitive aging. (Although a recent 2025 study from Russia found evidence of Semax injections reducing amyloid plaques in rat models of Alzheimer’s). Older studies using rats found improved cognition 15 minutes after injection, likely by stimulating BDNF production. There is a lack of safety data, especially in long-term side effects, in humans. One review reported discoloration of the nasal cavity and increased blood sugar levels in people with diabetes. Not great.

Selank is a nootropic touted for reducing anxiety and stress while increasing cognitive performance. Anecdotal evidence calls Selank a “life-changer” for anxiety and sleep, with some people feeling relaxed but not drowsy, as well as more focused.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Selank’s anxiolytic and cognitive protective effect along with relieving stress have only been studied in rodents and molecular studies. Older mice studies have also found evidence of improved learning and memory performance after a single injection of Selank.

TB-500 is a peptide intended for muscle recovery, increased flexibility, and joint stability. Users often pair the synthetic peptide with BPC-157 to further boost muscle recovery. TB-500 works by binding to a structural protein in cells called actin. By up-regulating actin, TB-500 purportedly speeds cell movement for tissue repair.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is a good amount of animal research on Thymosin Beta-4 and its accelerated healing effects on skin and muscle fibers. While there is a body of preclinical research on the peptide, there’s a lack of studies looking at the synthetic peptide TB-500. Plus, there is no clinical evidence in humans that Thymosin Beta-4 or TB-500 repairs muscles or increases athletic performance.

More concerning are studies linking elevated Thymosin Beta-4 levels with the development of cancer. Through the same mechanisms that promote wound healing, Thymosin Beta-4 may enhance tumor angiogenesis, the process where cancer cells stimulate new blood vessels, which provides them oxygen and nutrients to grow and spread.

Known as the “Wolverine” or “Body Protection Compound,” the synthetic peptide reportedly helps with tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects. Users champion the peptide’s ability to speed recovery from intensive workouts or even injury. BPC-157 does not directly build muscle mass.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Animal data on BPC-157 showed evidence of the peptide helping with musculoskeletal injuries. However, there is little data showing the effects in humans.

The natural form of this peptide helps with increasing and restoring immune function. It works by enhancing antibody response and T-cell activity. People taking the synthetic, injectable form report immediate improvement in their well-being after long COVID and other immune disorders. Outside of the US, Thymosin Alpha-1 is approved in over 30 countries for treating hepatitis and other infections.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Five large clinical trials on the peptide have found Thymosin Alpha-1 reduces inflammation and infection in people with severe acute pancreatitis. That’s likely due to the peptide’s ability to rebalance immune cell distribution, including boosting the percentages of CD4+ T cells. Thymosin Alpha-1 has also been shown to enhance vaccine response and help people with severe COVID by repairing damage caused by inflammation. However, one large phase 3 clinical trial in people with sepsis found an injection of thymosin alpha 1 did not improve mortality outcomes.

People taking the synthetic form of this peptide report doing so to reduce inflammation and improve skin health. (Some say it can clear up eczema, psoriasis, and acne.) There are also some people with inflammatory bowel conditions, such as Crohn’s and IBD, who say that KPV has helped their gut health. The peptide reportedly works by inhibiting several pro-inflammatory pathways while preserving other immune responses.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There’s not sufficient data on KPV to conclusively say it helps in humans. The most cited research on KPV is a 2008 study, which found that the peptide reduced intestinal inflammation in human intestinal cells. Yes, that was many, many years ago.

This neuropeptide reportedly promotes falling asleep faster, as well as increasing how much time you spend in restorative deep, slow-wave sleep. in Stage 3 sleep. Anecdotal evidence of people taking the synthetic form of this peptide states that in helps with staying asleep, increasing sleep duration, and entering deep sleep.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: DSIP research on humans is extremely limited. Most research looking into DSIP’s role in sleep took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed results. While a small clinical trial did report sleep-promoting effects, other studies found it ineffective or from a placebo effect. Research in the 2000s has been focused on animals and how DSIP could help protect against cancer or improve motor ability after stroke.

This peptide has links to sexual function. It works by stimulating the release of the hormone, gonadotropin, which results in an increase of testosterone. People who take synthetic kisspeptin-10 have reported a greater libido, ability to maintain an erection, and enjoy orgasm, along with reduced anxiety—especially surrounding sexual response.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is animal and human research that shows kisspeptin-10 stimulates gonadotrophin release. #4836. The Problem With Pain: Suffering and the Myth of Growth

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 1, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

A friend of ours recently totaled their car in an accident. The resulting concussion was worse. Concussions are never fun, but this one lingered.

It’s often said that pain can help us dig deep, find that extra gear, and become stronger, more resourceful people. Maybe. But pain can also lead us into a maze of suffering, with no clear sense of when, or whether, we’ll find our way out.

With some kinds of pain, we have a reasonable sense of what’s wrong and what recovery will look like. It hurts, but we expect it to pass.

Suffering can threaten our very sense of who we are. The distinction goes beyond the severity of the symptoms: it concerns what the experience means for us as people. Physician Eric Cassell described this threat to the person as central to suffering.

When we’re suffering, it can be hard to believe that what we’re experiencing is temporary. It could go on forever. And even if we come out the other side, will we come out intact? We may feel that something essential is being taken from us. We may question our purpose, see ourselves as burdens to loved ones, or feel that we’ve lost the capacity to care for ourselves or contribute to others. Suffering may begin with a physical injury, but its effects reach much further.

That’s what our friend is dealing with. The symptoms, the uncertainty, the disrupted routines, the inability to participate in work and social life as before.

So how should we support the people we care about who are suffering?

It’s not always clear. But putting pressure on them to be positive can worsen the burden. On top of what they’re already going through, they may feel added guilt for not handling it better. Research by Brock Bastian and colleagues suggests that feeling pressure not to experience negative emotions can make people feel worse. Post-traumatic growth seems like a big ask when someone is just trying to cope.

There’s also reason to be cautious about the claim that suffering makes us stronger. People sometimes report growth after trauma, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve changed in the ways they believe they have. In a prospective study of undergraduates, Patricia Frazier and colleagues found that reported growth generally did not correspond to changes measured before and after a traumatic event. The story we tell afterward may help us make sense of the experience, but that doesn’t mean it describes a measurable change.

And that’s OK. People can cope without growth. In two studies of people exposed to war or terrorism, Stephen Levine and colleagues found that participants with the greatest resilience reported the least post-traumatic growth. Here, the researchers defined resilience as the absence of post-traumatic stress disorder. People don’t need to emerge stronger to have coped well, and the process of coping may not leave much left in the tank.

Instead of asking them to change their perspective, we can start by taking their symptoms and suffering seriously. Listen without trying to supply a silver lining. Support modest, achievable goals that matter to them, while recognizing that their capacity may change from day to day. Help with practical burdens.

Specific help that addresses a concrete need is often easier for them to accept. Take care of an errand. Bring over a casserole. Keep it simple, too; don’t make your friend have to organize your assistance. And remember: they may be in that maze for a while. That means they may still need help long after the initial attention has faded.

When we offer encouragement, it should be concrete and credible. Acknowledge something they’ve managed or a difficulty they’ve faced. We don’t have to make the situation sound cheerful or promise that everything will work out.

We can care about their recovery without requiring them to find a lesson in it. And we can keep showing up while they find their own way through.

#4834. Can the BPC-157 ‘Wolverine’ Peptide Really Help With Pain and Recovery?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wellness seekers are increasingly turning to BPC-157, the wildly popular “Wolverine” peptide for injury recovery and pain relief, despite scant human evidence.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted in July to ease restrictions on it and several other peptides, recommending the injectable substances be made eligible for pharmacy compounding.

But before restrictions were eased, preliminary research suggests a rise in the use of the Wolverine peptide in recent years.

A September 2026 preprint analyzed more than 15 million medical records and identified 1,039 people with documented BPC-157 use.

The researchers found a roughly 33-fold increase in new users between 2020 and 2026.

The results, which were based on clinical records, have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

“The study found that BPC-157 use is largely hidden in clinical narrative rather than conventional prescription data,” said lead study author Venky Soundararajan, PhD, co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of nference.

“The proportion of newly documented BPC-157 users who were male rose from 57% in 2020 to 70% in 2026, a statistically significant trend,” he told Healthline.

“The user population for BPC-157 peptide is increasingly male in proportion and increasingly younger with each passing year.”

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide marketed and sold online for wellness.

Health claims about it and other peptides have spread on social media and in fitness circles and wellness communities, with high-profile advocates like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. touting their benefits.

Proponents of BPC-157 claim the injectable peptide promotes injury recovery, pain relief, and tissue healing. Some advocates claim that “stacking” the Wolverine peptide, particularly with TB-500, may enhance its effects.

The “Wolverine” peptide got its nickname from claims that it facilitates rapid healing, echoing the regenerative abilities of the fictional X-Men character of the same name.

This promise of pain relief and recovery may be what gives the Wolverine peptide its appeal.

Soundararajan’s study found that nearly 33% of patients reported using BPC-157 for pain relief. By comparison, just 4% of patients reported using BPC-157 for performance enhancement.

Across the cohort of 1,039 patients, 27% reported improvements.

“Pain relief was the dominant reported benefit, documented in 183 patients,” Soundarajan said. “Wound or tissue healing was reported in 38 patients and functional return in 34 patients.”

“Part of BPC-157’s appeal appears to be to patients who remain symptomatic after chronic, complex or previously treated musculoskeletal problems, signaling a clear clinical unmet need,” he said.

Bert Mandelbaum, MD, a sports medicine specialist, orthopedic surgeon, and co-director of the Regenerative Orthobiologic Center at Cedars-Sinai Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, said that everyone experiences pain, but warned about the risks of using the Wolverine peptide to treat it.

“There is zero indication that BPC-157 has any efficacy for pain,” he told Healthline. “There’s zero evidence that shows that it’s good for clinical healing, and we don’t really understand the safety profile of it.”

Human evidence of the possible benefits and safety of the Wolverine peptide is limited.

A 2025 systematic review of current BPC-157 literature found that it was dominated by preclinical research and low-grade human evidence. The review authors said there was insufficient clinical safety data to determine the peptide’s risks.

A small 2021 retrospective study on the effects of injectable BPC-157 on knee pain suggests the peptide could help repair tissue and regrow cartilage. However, the study followed just 16 participants, lacked a control group, and did not assess impacts on function or quality of life.

An even smaller 2025 intravenous safety pilot on BPC-157 use involved 2 participants. While no adverse effects were reported during the short study, the researchers acknowledged that larger studies are needed to confirm safety.

The July 23–24 FDA advisory vote added BPC-157 to the Section 503A bulk drug substances list, allowing pharmacies to include it in compounded medications.

The FDA’s 8-6 vote, with one abstention, greenlit BPC-157 in both free-base and acetate forms.

The recommendation did not make BPC-157 an FDA-approved drug, nor is it a component of an approved product. The federal health agency has yet to make final regulatory decisions on peptides.

“RFK Jr. policies are hurting Americans,” Mandelbaum said.

“This decision is ridiculous. It’s another step in the wrong direction. There’s no basis for any of this stuff.”

The safety profile of the Wolverine peptide for use in humans is largely unknown.

As such, BPC-157 is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency as an unapproved substance for athletes both in and out of competition.

The FDA notes that peptides like BPC-157 (free base) may be sensitive to product formulation, processing, environmental conditions, and impurities, which could degrade the products and reduce their effectiveness.

The health agency adds that it currently has limited safety information for how peptides like BPC-157 are administered.

Soundararajan explained that his study was unable to estimate the incidence or overall safety of BPC-157 because adverse events were captured retrospectively from routine clinical notes and are likely underreported.

“That said, the medical records examined contain both positive and negative patient experiences,” he said.

“Mood, sleep, skin, injection-site, and gastrointestinal symptoms are concrete safety outcomes among the few examined patient records with available evidence that deserve prospective measurement and discussions by healthcare providers with their patients who report using BPC-157.”

Some experts warn of short-term risks like infection at the injection site, but the long-term effects are not known.

“We don’t have publications of infections yet, but there are anecdotes of this,” Mandelbaum said.

“People are injecting their joints with this stuff, and you have no idea what it is. It’s not standardized. It’s not being regulated by the FDA, and I think people should recognize that. And although we haven’t proven it’s a safety hazard, we know it has no efficacy. So why do it? Why waste your money?”

Experts urge anyone considering BPC-157 or another peptide treatment to discuss it with their doctor first.

You might ask for evidence supporting its use, information on its quality, and whether there are alternatives with established safety and effectiveness profiles.

Mandelbaum noted there are many scientifically proven and safe alternatives to consider.

“We have spent the last 20 years developing an arsenal of biologics from PRP to bone marrow aspirate to adipose tissue to understanding glucosamine and hyaluronic acid,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job at studying these things. We’re getting to the point where we are understanding the complexities of biologics. It’s exciting, and it’s impactful.”

Mandelbaum vehemently opposed the use of unapproved peptides like BPC-157.

He likened its rise in popularity to a “Ponzi scheme” promoted by “gym rats” and “internet influencers” who “leverage and exploit the gap between hope and knowledge.” Just because the FDA eased restrictions, he said, doesn’t make them any safer or more legitimate.

That said, any use of unapproved peptides should also be disclosed to a doctor.

“A short, open and empathetic clinical conversation can turn invisible consumer use of products like BPC-157 into useful clinical information that can critically help inform current and future care for such patients that ensure the best possible outcomes,” Soundararajan said.

BPC-157 should not be combined with other experimental peptides until research determines the potential for adverse reactions or events. Long-term use of BPC-157 and other peptides marketed for wellness is not advised.

#4831. Volkswagen tells ID.4 owners to limit charging to 80% as part of a recall, or it will do it for them

Volkswagen told certain ID.4 drivers to limit charging to 80% as part of a recall by October 21. Unless drivers opt out, VW will automatically “apply a temporary vehicle setting” remotely.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs model years 2023 to 2026.

In a letter sent to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on October 6, Volkswagen urged owners to only charge their vehicles to a maximum of 80% battery capacity until a fix is ready.

Although the root cause is still unknown, Volkswagen said that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation,” or a fire within the battery.

In an email sent to owners with vehicles included in the recall, Volkswagen said that unless they opt out by October 21, it “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%.” The update will be done remotely and reflected in the mobile app on or about October 27, 2026.

You can accept or decline the change in the myVW app by selecting Accept Setting or Decline Setting by October 21. It will be shown as a 93EX High-Voltage Battery Settings notification.

Several ID.4 owners are already receiving the update. The recall follows a field study as part of an ongoing review of Volkswagen vehicles not included in previous battery recalls.

Volkswagen Group’s Product Safety Committee requested “additional clarifications” from the battery cell supplier, SK Battery America, about production and a potential clean date.

In the US, the company said it had received 22 claims between January 18, 2024, and August 07, 2026.

Volkswagen is still working on a remedy. Letters informing owners of the safety risks are expected to be mailed out on November 27, 2026. Once a fix is available, VW will send additional letters.

Owners can contact Volkswagen’s customer service at 1-800-893-5298 with questions or concerns. VW’s recall number is 93EX.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit NHTSA.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V630.

Volkswagen’s recall extends beyond the US market. A company spokesperson told the German newspaper Handelsblatt that “several thousand” Volkswagen Group EVs are affected, including the ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID. Buzz, and the Cupra Born.

Update 10/21/2026: Volkswagen recalls nearly 73,000 EVs globally (read more).

#4830. Increasing Ozempic Dose Linked to Lower Heart Risk Than Switching to Mounjaro

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Increasing the dose of Ozempic rather than switching to Mounjaro may be associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), according to a 2026 insurance claims analysis presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting 2026 in Milan, Italy.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) have reshaped care for people with type 2 diabetes, but recent real-world evidence suggests these drugs may not offer identical heart protection.

It is important to keep in mind that this was a retrospective, observational study that showed an association, not causation.

More research is needed to fully compare the cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide versus tirzepatide.

The COMPETE SWITCH Cardiovascular (CV) analysis used Komodo Health’s Healthcare Map, a large US healthcare claims database with linked laboratory results, to examine real-world data from 636,525 adults with type 2 diabetes.

The analysis focused on 185,705 people who increased their semaglutide dose and 23,104 who switched to tirzepatide.

All participants included in the analysis were already receiving 1 mg of semaglutide (Ozempic) weekly.

The researchers found that people who increased their Ozempic dose to 2 mg had a 6% lower risk of MACE — including all-cause death, myocardial infarction (heart attack), and stroke — compared with those who switched to Mounjaro at doses up to 15 mg.

“This is an interesting study, but the findings may partly reflect medication adherence. When patients switch medications, it can take time to adjust the dose and find the right treatment level, which may temporarily affect how well their condition is controlled,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

He also noted that the study did not determine what might explain the difference in cardiovascular risk.

“It may be related to a combination of weight loss and direct effects on hormones involved in metabolism and appetite regulation,” Ali said.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both GLP-1 medications. Ozempic (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are approved to help manage type 2 diabetes, while each medication also has a different brand approved for weight loss.

The semaglutide approved for weight loss in the U.S. is sold as Wegovy, and the tirzepatide approved for weight loss is sold as Zepbound.

“Semaglutide and tirzepatide work in a similar way. While semaglutide is a direct GLP-1 receptor agonist, tirzepatide is a dual agonist of both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors,” Amit Blumfield, MD, with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

“Because they work through somewhat different pathways, they can have different effects in individual patients,” added Ali.

While both semaglutide (Ozemipc) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) work in similar ways, you may find that you tolerate one better than the other.

Ali noted that you should discuss any potential benefits and drawbacks with your healthcare professional.

“I would only recommend switching medications if there is an issue with tolerance of one or the other. If one medication is well-tolerated at increasingly higher doses and is effective in the desired weight-loss and blood sugar management, I wouldn’t necessarily switch,” added Blumfield.

These side effects are generally mild and may lessen over time. However, if side effects become difficult to tolerate, you should speak with your healthcare professional.

“GLP-1 medications can be highly effective for managing diabetes and promoting weight loss, but there is no one-size-fits-all treatment. The best medication depends on an individual’s health needs, goals, response to treatment, and potential side effects,” said Ali.

#4828. Subaru is killing off gas cars and will only sell EVs in Europe

Subaru is phasing out combustion-engine vehicles in Europe by the end of 2027 and will sell only EVs.

The Japanese automaker will stop selling internal combustion engine vehicles in Europe by the end of next year, at the latest.

Known for its boxer engines, Subaru’s shift to an all-electric lineup is not necessarily by choice. Subaru Germany confirmed the news to Auto Motor und sport, saying the decision is due to the European Union’s emissions and driver-assistance regulations.

The transition will start with the Outback, Subaru’s iconic wagon, which will be discontinued at the end of the year.

In 2027, three more boxer-powered models will follow, including the Impreza, Crosstrek, and Forester, all of which use Subaru’s mild-hybrid 2.0L boxer engine.

From 2028, three EVs will remain in Subaru’s European lineup: the Solterra, E-Outback, and Uncharted. The three electric crossover SUVs are developed with Toyota and are twins of the bZ4X, bZ4X Touring, and C-HR+.

Subaru is not ruling out full hybrid drive vehicles for Europe at some point, but has no official plans yet.

The decision only applies to Europe. In the US, Subaru still sells the Crosstrek and Forester with a 2.5L full hybrid boxer engine.

Subaru’s US electric vehicle lineup consists of the Solterra, Uncharted, and Trailseeker, which is sold as the E-Outback in Europe. Next year, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getway. It’s essentially a rebadged version of Toyota’s three-row electric SUV, the Highlander BEV.

Well, not much of a change then. Subaru (market share ~0.2%) doesn't really sell any gas cars in the EU right now either.

Good luck to them - the European market is very competitive. In DK, Subaru's best selling vehicle, the Solterra, sold 172 units this year so far (rank 138) - slightly behind the overall top seller (Skoda Elroq, 7181 units).

Separately, Subaru showcased its first in-house EV tech to reporters on Sunday as it plans to wean off its reliance on Toyota for its next-generation electric vehicles.

The new tech includes Subaru’s first dedicated EV platform, plus new batteries, electric motors, and an integrated control unit to enable over-the-air updates.

Subaru didn’t reveal a specific launch date, but company officials said some of the new EV tech will begin rolling out around 2029.

The company showcased a disguised Outback test vehicle fitted with an all-wheel-drive powertrain that delivered a combined 509 horsepower (380 kW). According to Subaru, the setup is lighter, more efficient, and enables the EV to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under 4 seconds.

#4827. Oral GLP-1 Orforglipron (Foundayo) Achieves Weight Loss for Women of All Ages

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new GLP-1 pill called orforglipron (Foundayo) has been shown to help women lose weight, regardless of menopausal status, according to new research.

A group of researchers, including senior author Hunter Thomas Hoffman, PharmD, a clinical research scientist affiliated with the drug’s manufacturer, Eli Lilly, analyzed data from two prior trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, to arrive at this conclusion.

These studies reveal that this medication works equally well for women who have not yet gone through menopause, those who are currently experiencing it, and those who are postmenopausal.

The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), held in Milan, Italy, from September 28 to October 2.

This is important because menopause often causes weight gain due to lower estrogen levels, making weight loss more difficult for many women.

Orforglipron offers a promising new option for managing weight in women with obesity or overweight, especially those with type 2 diabetes.

In April of this year, Eli Lilly’s Foundayo received FDA approval as a weight-loss drug, making it the second GLP-1 pill for weight loss to enter the U.S. market after Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy.

The ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies involved women who were either obese or overweight and who had at least one medical condition related to their weight.

Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, and overweight as a BMI of 27 or higher.

The participants were divided into groups based on their menopausal status: premenopausal (before menopause), perimenopausal (during the menopause transition), and postmenopausal (after menopause).

Each group included between 142 and 225 females who either received orforglipron or placebo, an inactive pill with none of the drug in it.

The ATTAIN-1 study focused on people who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes. ATTAIN-2 included participants who had both overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The purpose of analyzing these two groups separately was to understand how orforglipron works in people with different health conditions.

The researchers measured several outcomes over a period of 72 weeks. They examined changes in body weight, waist circumference (the distance around the waist), and the waist-to-height ratio, a measure used to assess body fat distribution.

They also tracked how many women reached specific weight loss goals, such as losing at least 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% of their body weight, compared to those who took the inactive pill.

By studying these factors, the researchers were able to determine not only whether orforglipron helped women lose weight but also how much weight loss was achieved and how it affected their body shape.

The results showed that women who took orforglipron experienced significant weight loss regardless of their menopausal status.

In the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies, premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal women all lost an average of up to 14% of their body weight.

This means that the medication was effective for women at different life stages, including those experiencing menopause, when weight gain is often a challenge.

In addition to losing body weight, women in the orforglipron groups also saw meaningful reductions in waist circumference. Waist measurements decreased by up to 12.5 centimeters (about 5 inches) across all menopausal groups in both studies.

This reduction is important because greater visceral fat is associated with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

The waist-to-height ratio also improved for many women taking orforglipron. More participants treated with the medication moved into lower waist-to-height ratio categories than those who took the placebo.

This indicates a healthier distribution of body fat and suggests a lower risk of heart disease.

When looking at the number of women who reached specific weight loss milestones, orforglipron performed much better than the placebo. Up to 83% of women on orforglipron lost at least 5% of their body weight, while 30% of women on placebo reached that same level of weight loss.

Losing 5% or more of body weight is often considered clinically meaningful, as it can lead to improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.

Overall, these findings suggest that orforglipron is a promising new medication for weight management in women with obesity or overweight, including those who also have type 2 diabetes.

This can be especially helpful for those navigating the challenges of menopause while trying to manage their weight.

James J. Chao, MD, FACS, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of VedaNu Wellness, wasn’t involved in the research, but said the significance of these findings for postmenopausal women.

“The 14% is what’s grabbing headlines,” he told Healthline, “but up to 12.5 cm from the waistline is what I’m interested in.”

According to Chao, as females enter postmenopause, they tend to store more fat around their midsection.

“This is the type of fat that can cause heart disease,” he said. “So a pill that can help a 38-year-old woman lose the same amount as a 62-year-old breaks that myth.”

Additionally, in contrast to most GLP-1 drugs, which are injectable, it’s a once-a-day pill. You can also take it any time, Chao explained, making it more convenient.

“No needle, no refrigerator, and up to 83% of participants lost at least 5%,” he said. “Sometimes it’s the simple things that make a difference.”

Luca Moretti, MD, a medical doctor at Sapienza University of Rome, who wasn’t involved in the studies, added that convenience isn’t the only thing to consider when deciding whether to use orforglipron.

Obesity management should begin with an individualized plan that includes nutrition, physical activity, and the management of other risk factors.

“When these measures are not sufficient, adding pharmacological treatment can be considered together with a physician,” he told Healthline.

Moretti further advised speaking with your physician about any potential side effects, your existing medical conditions, other medications you are taking, and your treatment preferences.

“So the most useful question to ask a doctor is not simply, ‘Is Foundayo more convenient?’ but rather: ‘Among the available treatments, which one offers the best balance of effectiveness, tolerability, and practicality for me?'” he said.

#4825. Is the Documentary "You Can See Everything" Inaccurate?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 1, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

The A24 (meta-) documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the now-defunct health technology company Theranos, got the internet abuzz. If you watch it, you will see why. The feature is both thought-provoking and unusual, and the main subjects featured in it—Holmes and her partner Billy Evans—have the screen presence of highly-paid actors playing Holmes and Evans.

As one might expect amid so much attention, there are criticisms as well. A key objection made is that the film is inaccurate. One can see why some people think that. There is, for instance, a scene in the film in which Holmes and one of the directors, Nathan Fielder, debate the meaning of the word “can” in the expression “can run every test.” Holmes insists that the device she is showing to Fielder “can run every test.” Fielder suggests that Holmes is not using the word “can” in the usual way. (Note: In one sense of “can,” I can defeat the world chess champion at chess, namely, it is not physically impossible for me to move the pieces on the board so as to score a victory. But if I say I can defeat the world chess champion, you will take me to be saying something different and altogether false. It may also be that Holmes’ device can run every test in some such sense. That, of course, is not the sense that would have interested either customers or investors.) In another scene, Holmes is shown Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First?” comedy sketch, and she seems to either not get or pretend not to get the joke, which involves understanding that “Who,” “What," and “I Don’t Know” are names of baseball players.

These and other scenes may leave viewers with the impression that Holmes simply doesn’t use words in the way most people do, and that perhaps, she is not so much a fraudster as a highly idiosyncratic language user with less-than-stellar communication skills.

Were that the message, the film would be, indeed, inaccurate. Holmes is not in prison because of miscommunication. She falsified financial records, diluted people’s blood with water and had the samples analyzed by real labs then claimed to have used the Theranos device, and she did other similar things.

However, I am not inclined to view the film as misleading, because I don’t know what, if anything, it is asserting. A conventional documentary asserts—i.e., invites audiences to believe—various claims about the characters and events it depicts, and if the claims asserted are false, the documentary is, to that extent, inaccurate. But You Can See Everything is not a conventional documentary. For one thing, Fielder mentions at the very beginning that he is not “good at science things” and asks Holmes whether that was why she invited him and not someone else better equipped to ask questions about the technology. This can be taken as a disclaimer on his part: Viewer beware.

No less importantly, Fielder and Oppenheim could have spoken to other people better-versed in both the science and in the details of the case. This is what one might get in a conventional documentary. Fielder and Oppenheim do not do that either, and the choice seems deliberate. That too may be taken as a signal to the viewer that the filmmakers did not intend to explain “what really happened.”

One can argue, perhaps, that in engaging with Holmes in a discussion about the meaning of “can,” Fielder was deliberately introducing ambiguity to make the story more interesting. But I am not sure that’s true either. An alternative interpretation is this: Fielder wanted to see how far he could get with Holmes if he played on her turf and started from her own premises. Suppose she really did use the word “can” in an atypical way. Shouldn’t she have nonetheless anticipated that this would lead to a misunderstanding? As for the Abbott and Costello sketch, that may have been bait to see what Holmes would say about it. She can be seen laughing while watching it. That suggests she understood what’s funny. What would she say if asked? She denies she understood. The documentary does not assert that her denial is in good faith. An alternative interpretation is that we see Holmes seizing the opportunity and trying to pull the veil over our eyes while falling for Fielder’s trick.

I, for one, am very glad that Fielder and Oppenheim took the approach they took. The actual story has been covered previously, and more than once. The world doesn’t need another run-of-the-mill Holmes documentary, however accurate. What You Can See Everything offers, instead, is an attempt to penetrate what looks like Holmes’ façade. It does not succeed despite the fact that the team has full access for an extended period of time. It is a bit as though the lodgers with their cameras keep knocking on the door even though they are already inside the house. They never get behind the immaterial partition which separates them from the thoughts of their subjects. Just why that is is one of the themes of the film.

In a widely viewed trailer, Holmes is heard saying to Fielder, “I am engaging with you as a human being” and “I am always being real.” It is really the filmmakers who seem to want to engage with Holmes as a human being, but they only get her to reflect their own intentions back at them. Since their main goal was to create an entertaining feature and they succeeded at that, perhaps, we can hand them the victory. But Holmes’ own play remains a mystery, so one could say they succeed on Homes' terms. In the game of manipulation, Holmes and the film-makers draw.

The feature is unconventional—though, importantly, not in a way that’s parasitic on prior conventions, as when an “invisible” artwork seeks to thwart the expectation that artworks in general have some material bearer. The movie feels genuinely original. It surprises viewers without trying to trick them by leading them to expect one thing and giving them another. The work is exploratory, too. It doesn’t promise to deliver anything in particular—least of all, “the truth about Holmes”—but it delivers.

Precisely what it is that it delivers is not easy to say, but that’s part of its point—and its charm.

I would not call the film inaccurate. Of course, it isn’t accurate either. It is something else.

#4823. Switching from GLP-1 Injections to Wegovy Pill Shows Additional Weight Loss of 4.1%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People with overweight or obesity who switch from an injectable GLP-1 medication to the Wegovy (semaglutide) pill may continue to lose weight, according to findings from the OCTANE study presented at the 2026 Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

The study is among the first real-world analyses to examine weight loss and treatment experiences among people who switched from an injectable weight loss medication to oral semaglutide (Wegovy).

However, while real-world studies like this can provide useful insights into how treatments work in everyday life, these findings do not prove that switching to the Wegovy pill caused the weight loss.

The results have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

This was a retrospective cohort analysis evaluating weight change, treatment adherence, and patient satisfaction after people switched from injectable semaglutide (Wegovy) or tirzepatide (Zepbound) to oral semaglutide for weight management.

The study included a random sample of 194 adults with overweight or obesity and at least one obesity-related complication, such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and dyslipidemia.

Participants had no history of diabetes or bariatric surgery and had an average baseline weight of 221.6 pounds (100.5 kg) and an average body mass index (BMI) of 34.5 kg/m2.

Participants switched from an injectable GLP-1 medication to oral semaglutide between January 5 and February 7, 2026. There was no requirement for how long they had used an injectable medication or how much weight they had lost before switching.

Participants were required to use oral semaglutide regularly for 3 months and self-report their weight within 30 days of starting treatment and again at the end of the study period.

After 3 months of taking oral semaglutide, participants had lost an average of 4.1% of their body weight, or 8.8 pounds.

At the 3-month mark, 2 in 5 participants (40.7%) had lost 5% or more of their body weight.

The proportion of participants with a BMI of 30 or greater also decreased by 21.6 percentage points, from 87.1% at baseline to 65.5% after 3 months.

Most participants (82.4%) reported at least one treatment improvement. Around 69% reported better-fitting clothes, and around 51% reported eating healthier.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Medical Director, Diabetes & Metabolic Center at University Hospitals, Cleveland, OH, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that, “These findings are encouraging because they suggest that some people can continue losing weight after switching to oral treatment.”

However, she also noted, “I would view this as promising early evidence supporting another treatment option, rather than proof that switching improves results.”

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted that because the oral medication is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, less of it reaches the bloodstream compared to the injectable form.

However, oral semaglutide can still be effective for weight loss.

“While studies show that the injectable form is more efficacious, current findings demonstrate that the oral version is also effective for weight loss,” said Ali.

Some people may prefer the oral form for ease of use and transportation because it does not require refrigeration. However, it must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach, followed by a 30-minute wait before eating, Ali told Healthline.

“Both formulations can cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Taking a pill does not eliminate those risks,” Hatipoglu said.

Hatipoglu also said factors to consider include how well your current treatment is working, side effects, your comfort with injections, your daily routine, cost, and insurance coverage.

She added that the decision should be made with a prescribing clinician, who can help plan the transition and monitor your response.

“Both options can be effective, so patients should discuss the risks and benefits of each with their provider. Ultimately, these medications are tools to support a healthier diet and lifestyle, and patients who make these fundamental changes achieve the best results,” said Ali.

#4822. BMW iX5 hits up to 460 kW during first public fast-charging demo

With up to 460 kW DC fast charging, the new BMW iX5 can add up to 170 miles in just 10 minutes. BMW proved it during a live public event for the first time.

BMW’s new electric vehicles are a step change from its previous-generation EVs. Based on its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system with 800V technology, the setup delivers up to a 30% increase in driving range and charging speeds compared to the Gen5 system.

In addition to new, highly efficient electric motors, the Gen6 eDrive uses new batteries with cylindrical cells that BMW says provide 20% greater energy density than the Gen5 prismatic cells.

To prove just how fast it can charge, BMW put the new iX5 50 xDrive to the test during an international media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW, even slightly higher than the 460 kW that BMW reported.

BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the 144 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

While the results are impressive, 460 kW is the peak rate, not the sustained rate during the entire charging session. Either way, it’s still impressive and quick enough to get you back on the road quickly.

The vehicle averages over 280 kw across the 10%-80% range. That is a sustained rate faster than the peak charging of most vehicles. The 450 miles of range means it will add 315 EPA miles in less than 22 min. Impressive for any vehicle available in the US.

Plus, the US does not have the hardware to support 460 kW charging. Alpitronic supplied the hardware, and the demo was at an IONNA charger.

BMW will launch the 2027 iX5 60 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800. Official EPA figures are still pending, but BMW estimates the iX5 will offer up to 435 miles of range with a 144 kWh battery.

It’s powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, which BMW says enables it to go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.

The new iX5 is BMW’s first all-electric vehicle produced in the US. BMW is set to begin production at its Plant Spartanburg by the end of the year.

#4821. Detached Nails More Than 4 Times Higher Among GLP-1 Users, Study Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have reported various unusual side effects like “Ozempic feet,” “Ozempic butt,” and “Ozempic breasts.” These changes have been largely tied to rapid weight loss.

Now, fingernails have entered the conversation. Nails detaching from the nail bed or changing color may be more common among people taking GLP-1 drugs, according to a new study. In the study, which researchers presented in October at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, people taking GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide — Ozempic, Wegovy — and tirzepatide — Mounjaro, Zepbound — reported nail detachment and nail discoloration more often than people who didn’t take the drugs.

When the researchers counted only nail changes that started after treatment began, the link between GLP-1 use and nail detachment nearly disappeared, study author Charles Taïeb, MD, PhD, told Healthline.

“This is why we insist that a substantial part of the nail excess reflects the patients’ overall health rather than the drug itself, while a modest drug-specific effect remains plausible,” Taïeb said.Earlier research has also linked GLP-1 use to hair loss. In the new study, the researchers explained why they examined nails, noting that nails and hair both grow from cells that divide quickly.

However, the researchers cautioned in a press release that the study can’t establish that the drugs caused the nail changes. Both the nail study and a companion hair study captured self-reported symptoms at a single point in time, a design that can identify associations only, they said.

For the study, researchers examined a representative sample of people in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.

Participants included 575 people taking GLP-1 drugs and 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes, obesity, or both conditions, who had never taken GLP-1 drugs.

The average treatment duration was 18.5 months, and researchers tracked weight loss over three months.

They also looked separately at people who had lost weight, to help tell whether the drugs or the weight loss explained the changes. However, the abstract didn’t specify which GLP-1 drugs participants took.

The researchers have submitted the findings to peer-reviewed dermatology journals, where they are under review, Taïeb told Healthline. Here’s what they found.

According to the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), nail detachment, or onycholysis, occurs when a nail lifts, and the lifted area often appears white.

Taïeb told Healthline that the study asked about “nail detachment” because patients, not doctors, filled out the questionnaire. Nail detachment was the strongest signal among the five nail changes the researchers asked about, Taïeb said.

According to the abstract, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail separation or detachment (onycholysis), compared with 9% of nonusers.

Nail discoloration is a change in a nail’s usual color, such as white, yellow, or greenish-black, according to the AAD.According to the abstract, 46% of GLP-1 users reported discoloration, compared with 17% of nonusers. Ridges or grooves and fragile nails were also more common among GLP-1 users.

Mir B. Ali, MD, a bariatric surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Los Angeles, said that while he prescribes GLP-1s, nail detachment hasn’t come up in his practice. Ali wasn’t involved in the research.“I haven’t had anybody complain of that. It’s not something we really see,” he told Healthline. He said his patients more often mention brittle nails or minor changes in nail color.

Over a three-month period, 76% of GLP-1 users reported weight loss, compared with 47% of nonusers, according to the abstract.Weight loss alone didn’t appear to explain the nail findings, the researchers said in the press release. The differences between users and nonusers held up when they looked only at people who had lost weight.The researchers also cautioned in the press release that the study can’t show the drugs caused the changes. They noted that about half of GLP-1 users had nail problems before starting treatment.

Adjusting for skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies weakened some of the associations, they said, though nail detachment and discoloration stayed about two to three times as common among users.Those adjustments relied on conditions participants reported, including iron, vitamin B12, zinc, and vitamin D deficiencies, as well as psoriasis, eczema, and other skin conditions, Taïeb said.“GLP-1 medications may affect the nails indirectly rather than directly,” said Tanya Evans, MD, a board certified dermatologist and medical director of the Skin Cancer Program at the Melanoma Clinic at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, who wasn’t involved in the research.Because the drugs reduce appetite, some people may eat less protein, iron, and zinc, which can contribute to brittle nails, discoloration, or nail detachment, Evans told Healthline. Rapid weight loss may also temporarily disrupt nail growth, much as it can trigger hair shedding, she said.Ali said the total amount of weight a person loses plays a bigger role in hair and nail changes than the rate at which they lose it.

The U.S. labels for Wegovy and Zepbound list hair loss as a side effect reported in clinical trials.

The labels for the Ozempic, both injectable and pill form, as well as Mounjaro, list hair loss as a side effect, based on reports received after the drugs entered the market. Those reports don’t establish how often it happens or whether the drugs caused it.

As such, researchers have been examining GLP-1-related hair loss.

A companion study of the same participants found hair and scalp changes were also more common among GLP-1 users, according to that study’s abstract, also provided to Healthline:

Scalp redness was about three times as common among users, and most users with hair loss also had scalp symptoms such as itching, redness, or scaling.Scalp inflammation may play a role in hair changes among GLP-1 users, in addition to the shedding that often follows rapid weight loss, one of the study’s authors stated in the news release.“This raises the possibility that inflammation may be contributing in some patients, rather than the problem being solely the classic temporary hair shedding associated with rapid weight loss,” Evans said.Experts have told Healthline that hair loss on GLP-1 drugs is often temporary and tied to weight loss.“Hair loss, we see commonly, not only in patients who are on GLP-1 medications, but also in our surgical weight loss patients,” Ali said.

“When you lose weight, especially in women, it releases hormones. You’re getting metabolic changes, and all these things can lead to hair loss and some changes in the nails.” Ali said he tells patients that “as the weight stabilizes at a healthy weight, the hormones stabilize and the hair tends to come back to where it was before.”

Nail detachment and discoloration don’t appear as adverse reactions in the current U.S. prescribing information for Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound.

Ali said the best thing patients can do is get the right nutrition, including enough protein. He said he also advises patients to take a multivitamin along with B-complex, vitamin D, and calcium.

“I would not recommend stopping the GLP-1 medication simply because nail detachment occurs,” Evans said. She advised people to tell their doctor about any new changes in hair, scalp, or nails.Treatment for nail detachment or discoloration depends on the cause, Evans said. A dermatologist can check for an infection, an inflammatory nail disorder, a nutritional problem, an injury, or another explanation, she said.A detached nail recovers as a new nail grows out from its base, Evans said. That takes about 4 to 6 months for a fingernail and 9 to 12 months for a toenail.

Lastly, the AAD recommends having a board certified dermatologist examine any nail that’s lifting.

The AAD also recommends seeing a dermatologist if skin, hair, or nail side effects don’t improve, as they can help determine whether symptoms are due to the medication or another condition.“The important message is don’t panic, but don’t ignore persistent nail changes either,” Evans said.
