#4763. Swallowed by a Sea Monster: 'Whalefall' and Fatherhood

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

One of the best-known stories of the Bible is that of Jonah, a man who gets himself swallowed by a whale (actually, a “great fish”). Why this happens is probably less popularly understood. The reason is that Jonah has defied God. The Lord wanted him to go to the city of Nineveh and preach to the people there about their sins. He refused and sought escape to the city of Tarshish via a ship leaving from Joppa.

As you might imagine, God is not pleased. A storm arises from the sea, and the ship gets dangerously tossed about. When the crew draws lots to determine who is at fault, Jonah’s number comes up. He admits he is Hebrew and has defied God. He volunteers himself as a sacrifice, and they toss him overboard. As expected, the waters become calm.

What happens next is the part most of us know about. Jonah is swallowed by a sea monster. He suffers in “the belly of hell” for three days. Finally, God forgives him and talks to the fish, who “vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.” Jonah goes on to do what he was supposed to do, now wiser from the experience.

This story has burrowed deep into our cultural psyche. Famed psychologist Abraham Maslow found the tale so compelling he came up with a term: the Jonah Complex. To suffer this complex is to fail to follow one’s true calling. You deny yourself, and you will descend into a dark place, where, hopefully, you will realize your errors and return to your true life path. You’ll emerge from the belly of the beast you’d so recklessly volunteered for and find the bright light of day.

In a new movie, "Whalefall," a young man takes Jonah’s original harrowing route. He denies the grief he should be feeling over the death of his father by suicide. This boy has lived a tortured life, marked by a tough relationship with his father. A gruff old salt who’d led scuba tours, dad constantly berated his son for a lack of fortitude and insufficient love of the sea. Father and son fail to understand each other. It is a classic story of the alienation that can arise between “tough” dads and their sensitive sons. The sons feel they are not good enough, and the fathers know they are missing something, but can’t see through their own pain to do anything about it.

The idea that fathers no longer have the tools to raise their sons properly has long been a popular topic in pop psychology. Fathers, we have been told, are emotionally unavailable and do not know how to inculcate in their sons the proper virtues of self-sufficiency and human connection. Sadly, this argument often winds up blaming domineering “viper” mothers who suffocate their sons and diminish their husbands’ role.

"Whalefall" taps the ongoing cultural conversation of finding the father with a wild take on the Jonah story. The boy, on a solo scuba mission to recover remnants of dad (who chose to drown himself rather than wither away from lung cancer), gets swallowed by a sperm whale. The event, wild on its face, is filmed realistically.

Inside the whale, the boy experiences a trip to hell. The space is claustrophobic, the air is poisonous, and his wounds become more and more grievous. In this surreal space, we experience a series of flashbacks that sketch out the father’s failures and the son’s desire to connect with him. Ultimately, the whale itself becomes the father, and through conversation, the boy realizes that his dad did, in fact, love him, even if he could not show it. The whale-father ultimately supplies the boy with the tools to help him escape. Like the Jonah story, he is expelled from the beast to reach the light of day, transformed by his experience.

"Whalefall" offers the metaphorical father redemption arc that delivers a novel take on Maslow’s Jonah Complex. What dad was unable to do in life, he succeeds in doing through a dying sperm whale on the Pacific coast. The boy takes responsibility for his own life success, and the father can finally be properly grieved over. This film, while shot realistically, is in fact a mythic treatment of an enduring social problem. Does it succeed? That depends on the viewer.

Betts, J. "The Belly of the Whale." (Jan 19, 2013). Jungian Psychoanalysis. https://jungian.ca/articles/the-belly-of-the-whale/.

Cho, W. (Dec 6, 2017). "The Jonah Complex — Fear of Your Own Greatness." Medium. https://medium.com/student-voices/the-jonah-complex-fear-of-your-own-gr….

#4762. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4761. What Rest-Pause Training Can Do for Your Workout

A simple practice lets you push past failure—without lowering the weight.

TRY AS YOU might, you can’t pump out reps forever when you’re working toward building bigger muscles. Eventually, you‘ll be too fatigued to complete another rep with good form, a point referred to as “technical failure.” Pushing beyond your last good rep can lead to sloppy lifting mechanics, which can compromise your results or, worse increase your risk of injury. If you find yourself stuck lifting the same weight for the same reps, it may be time to get creative with how you push past that iron hurdle.

One way to head off the siren song of ego lifting is by implementing a planned rest-pause set. It’s an intense lifting technique that requires focus and intention, and as effective as it can be, it shouldn’t be done for every set or even every exercise.

By briefly resting after reaching failure, you can squeeze out a few more quality reps using the same weight. A few extra reps might not seem like a big deal, but they can add up over time, giving your muscles an extra dose of the tension that drives growth.

To do a rest-pause set, you’ll take an exercise to the point where you can’t complete another rep with good form. You’ll then rest for five to 15 seconds—in one MH workout plan, fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. recommends taking “three deep breaths” for a pause—then squeeze out a few more reps (expect to be able to do two to four) using the same weight. You can repeat this process, though one additional round of reps is a good starting point.

If you rest longer than 20 seconds, Alexander Rothstein, an exercise physiologist and program coordinator of exercise science at the New York Institute of Technology, says you’re starting to approach a standard rest interval. "If you give yourself that brief moment to… recover, and then you continue the set, you haven't flushed away all of the waste products, and you haven't fully recovered your energy stores, but you are still capable of doing a few more high-quality reps,” he explains.

The purpose of a rest-pause set is to push your muscle to complete a few more hard (but high-quality) reps. If you’re aiming to build muscle, it’s those hard reps near the end of a set that are key; a rest-pause set allows you to sneak in a few more of those reps. While lifters of any experience level can perform rest-pause sets, they’re especially useful for advanced lifters who’ve already cashed in their newbie gains and find it increasingly difficult to progress their lifts and add muscle.

Say you’re doing the dumbbell bench press, an exercise on which you’ve been stuck using the same 50-pound dumbbells for sets of 8 to 10 reps for over a month. You get to that 10th rep and, once again, can’t muster another. Instead of calling it this time, you’ll sit up, rest the dumbbells on your thighs for 15 seconds, and then bust out another two reps. Congrats. You just eked out more worthwhile reps, which, over time, should help you progress.

“But isn’t that cheating?” you ask. No—and even if it were, there are times when cheating pays off for muscle gains. And research suggests that traditional sets and rest-pause sets can produce similar gains in strength and muscle. One small study had 18 experienced lifters perform six weeks of traditional sets or rest-pause training with the same relative load. One group completed three sets of six reps; the other did one set to failure and then as many rest-pause sets as necessary to hit 18 reps. Both groups achieved similar strength gains, but the rest-pause group experienced greater increases in thigh muscle thickness and leg-press muscular endurance.

As for how to start using them, pick one exercise per workout—ideally, a move you’re struggling to progress—and do the final set of that exercise as a rest-pause set. This often works best with the final exercise in your workout. The rest-pause protocol can be downright exhausting, and using them too early may compromise your ability to hit your typical reps and weights during subsequent sets.

One note: You can perform rest-pause sets with just about any exercise, but there are two places where they’re especially beneficial. Weight machines are the safest, letting you easily push to fatigue, then take your brief “rest”. Exercises that offer support for stabilizing muscles (think: chest-supported rows) also work well. And many single-joint free-weight exercises, like dumbbell curls are good options. If you’re going to attempt a rest-pause set with the bench press or back squat, have a good spotter on hand.

There’s more than one way to increase the volume of a single set, and these methods are often referred to as intensity techniques. Below, we’ll briefly compare the three most popular ones to rest-pause sets.

A drop set is when you reach failure on a lift, then immediately reduce the load (often by 10 to 20 percent) and try to squeeze out a few more reps. In many ways, it’s similar to a rest-pause set, but because you’re lightening the weight, you’ll find it easier to maintain good form.

“Personally, I just like the volume approach of drop sets,” Rothstein says. "When you do drop sets, obviously the load is being reduced, so it's not as potentially strength beneficial as it might be to just do rest-pauses and still lift heavy loads."

A cluster set is when you break up a traditional straight set into a series of mini sets, or clusters, with short rest periods between each. They're a popular training method among strength athletes, such as powerlifters and weightlifters, who want to accumulate more total tonnage.

Say, for example, you can typically deadlift 250 pounds for eight reps. You could load 285 to 300 pounds on the bar and perform four two-rep clusters, resting 15 to 30 seconds between, to complete the same eight reps with roughly 15 to 20 percent more weight.

The main difference between rest-pause and cluster sets is that cluster sets strategically use rest to achieve a preplanned number of reps, often at a higher weight. Rest-pause sets have you take a few breaths after reaching failure to push past what you can normally do rep-wise. Cluster sets are likely superior to rest-pause sets for building strength.

Instead of resting and then doing more reps once you reach failure, you can perform forced reps, where your spotter provides just enough assistance to help you complete a few more reps with good form. Forced reps are usually done on exercises where a spotter can easily help; think the bench press or certain machine exercises, not deadlifts or heavy back squats.

While you’re technically pushing past failure, you don’t have control over how much assistance your spotter provides; this can vary from workout to workout or even rep to rep. You can, however, control the eccentric portion of the contraction after the spotter has helped you, so if you’re doing forced reps, it’s a must to lower the weight slowly to get the most from these. Forced reps can be a useful occasional technique if you have an experienced spotter who knows how much assistance to provide; because they’re forcing you to acclimate to increased time-under-tension with a weight that you know is challenging.

Ford opened orders for the 2027 Mustang Mach-E, which now offers a standard extended-range battery for under $40,000. A new Trail model is also joining the lineup.

Ford’s electric crossover SUV is back for another model year. The 2027 Mustang Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery.

The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-e is available in five trims: Select, Premium, GT, Rally, and a new purpose-built Trail model.

The new 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail is available for a $2,295 package upgrade for the Select eAWD.

According to Ford, the new Trail package is designed to make “outdoor adventures across pavement, gravel, and dirt roads more accessible than ever.”

It features fine-tuned front and rear struts and springs, a Rally-shaped steering rack, 19-inch High Gloss Dark Carbonized Gray Wheels with as-cast graphics, and is 10 mm taller in the front and 15 mm taller in the rear than the base Mach-E.

The 2027 Mustang Mach-E Trail comes with standard 400W, 120V Pro Power Onboard. It’s available as an upgrade for other variants, including the Premium, GT, and Mustang Mach-E Rally.

Select and Premium models use the 88 kWh battery and are available with rear- or all-wheel-drive (eAWD) powertrains. The GT and Rally variants use the 91 kWh battery and are only sold as eAWD models.

Ford’s BlueCruise 1.5 comes standard on the GT and Rally and optional on Select with Tech Pack Lite and Premium with Premium Tech Pack models. The Trail requires the hardware selection at the time of ordering. It cannot be added later.

Meanwhile, the Ford Connectivity Package and Ford Security Package are standard across the entire 2027 lineup.

The base 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Select RWD starts at $39,995. Including the $2,045 destination fee, prices start at $42,040.

While it is a bit more expensive than the 2026 model year, Ford no longer offers the standard-range battery. Ford said a new secondary front motor delivers the same performance as the previous unit but at a lower cost, enabling the lower-priced base RWD model with the extended-range battery.

We're at almost 80,000 miles in our Mach E GT and we'll drive it to 200,000+. It's a blast to drive and we've loved owning it. Feels as solid now as it did day 1.

Bought a set of summer tires at 43k miles. Other than that, and swapping between winter/summer tires, the maintenance cost has been $0.

We don't DC fast charge very often, so the slower L3 charging isn't a big deal for us - but does need improvement IMO.

Previously, the extended-range battery was available, starting at $45,345 on the 2026 Mustang Mach-E.

The extended-range (88 kWh) battery provides an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 320 miles in RWD models. Depending on the configuration, eAWD models offer 300 miles of range. The GT and Rally use the 91 kWh battery, providing 280 miles and 255 miles of range, respectively.

Ford will announce the final EPA-estimated driving range for the Trail model closer to when it goes on sale, expected in the first quarter of 2027.

#4759. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4758. Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B

Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”

Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”

Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.

The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”

There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.

Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:

Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.

The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.

Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.

Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.

Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.

If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.

The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.

Rearranging the deck chairs ahead of the merger?

None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.

Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.

The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

#4756. The 'Culting' of Mental Health Diagnosis

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

The Culting of Brands sounds like one of those polemical books about ad industry manipulation. It’s not. It’s a how-to.

In the early 2000s, marketers were contending with savvy consumers wary of advertising tactics. One marketer, Douglas Atkin, realized that some brands had managed to engender cult-like devotion in their customers that transcended advertising and products.

He studied these "culty" brands and actual cults to figure out how this could work. Cults ensnare smart, capable (and ideally influential) people, he argued, by offering a couple of core human desires: meaning and belonging. Cults enclose a worldview around their followers that pre-answers questions, arming devotees with deeply felt shared perspectives.

His book therefore recommends that brands provide ideologies and identities for consumers. Chapters include “You’re Different, We’re Different,” “You Belong,” “This Is What We Believe,” and “We Love You.”

Another brand strategy book, Lovemarks, asserts that tapping into emotion and helping people to tell the story of their lives through brand values (where disentangling from them would unravel the very story of the self) is key to obtaining loyalty beyond reason from customers.

I write about ways marketing messages have been conflated with medical ones in mental health, and how the emotional affordances of social media platforms enable spaces where we don’t just identify with common characteristics of disorders; we feel them.

Social media is invested in invoking and enlisting user moods, providing and platforming interpretations of those moods, encapsulating them in memes (and sometimes even selling them as user data). Using social media can mimic states we consider overstimulation, executive dysfunction, or dissociation. When TikTok content tells us that “doomscrolling” TikTok is itself a symptom of a disorder and that a therapy app has a solution, we are seeing and feeling content as designed. But diagnostic brands in themselves aren’t new.

A strategy employed by marketers of psychopharmaceuticals has been to sell the diagnosis, not the product. Accomplished through extensive PR campaigns, sponsored conferences, lobbying, screening and awareness initiatives, and other tactics focused on securing an enduring market, the diagnosis becomes the brand (see Healy, 2008; Horwitz, 2021). Product demand follows.

Direct-to-consumer psychopharmaceutical ads often point to a singular explanation for a complex condition—usually a theorized mechanism of a drug's therapeutic effect (a logic roughly akin to assuming social anxiety is an alcohol deficiency). Medication is an important treatment tool for many. Its marketing, however, can discount social, environmental, or even other possible biomedical factors in mental health.

Before medications required association with specific disorders to obtain approval on the market and before there were hundreds of possible diagnoses to link them to, ads in medical journals advised doctors that societal pressures and the pains of living in themselves called for psychiatric medications.

As troubling as some of these ads were (like plainly stating there was no escape for "subservient" 1950s housewives), they did not tend to position anything inherently wrong with people or brains (and drugs like Miltown had a cult brand following beyond being "mother's little helpers"). Today, promotional materials and influencers are more likely to reduce suffering to serotonin, dopamine, or to use totalizing medical analogies (“like insulin for a diabetic”), shaping treatment decisions and self-understanding.

The ubiquitous and scientifically shaky insulin metaphor brings to mind another brand cult strategy, per Atkin, of “shared language.” Social media provides “therapy speak"—a fusion of pop psychology, therapeutic, and loosely applicable clinical terms that structure understanding of ourselves and others.

Clinically, our mental health diagnoses were primarily designed to describe symptoms, not explain them. On social media, however, rather than opening up questions, diagnoses are the answers.

Why does she have these mood swings? Because she’s bipolar. Of course they’re gaslighting me; they’re a narcissist. Why do I feel depressed? I have depression. It’s algorithmically tautological, self-reinforcing, and rests upon frameworks that draw more from PR than psychology or medicine.

Diagnoses and related terms become all-encompassing explanations. Psychiatrist and cult scholar Robert Jay Lifton described “loading the language" as a way of “reducing every issue in a complicated life to a single set of slogans that are said to embody the truth as a totality.” These terms can also work to shut down other ways of discussing, explaining, or exploring our traumas, challenges, capacities, and relationships.

Beyond this, social media diagnosis also provides consumer services and products, as well as the endless scroll of therapeutic information. Promoting a problem alongside a lifelong consumer solution is another marketing staple.

Though loyalty beyond reason is not to specific products in this case, it is to the idea of the diagnosis and the associated worldview its marketing has cultivated. This includes diagnostic lore that arises from social media users themselves; positioning the customer as "co-author" of the brand is textbook marketing strategy.

Who benefits most from these emotionally imbued consumer diagnostic identities? Why do people fervently adopt and "trauma bond" to them? Can they meaningfully improve actual mental health?

I currently research mental health and media. I also teach classes in public relations, advertising, and social media, so I think a lot about this. Something one of my own counseling professors would repeat in class has stuck with me throughout: “Honor the defenses.”

With this in mind, I look at the social media diagnostic identities I write about here and in my book as a way of adapting within increasing demands that include branding oneself in a digital economy. A number of mental health symptoms and associated biomedical components can be viewed as responses that in some way developed to cope with intense stressors.

Finding communities through which to share stories of struggle and healing is a strength of social media and, not incidentally, of social media marketing. The ongoing challenge is to recognize aspects of diagnostic “brand cults” and to continually strive to prioritize mental health over platforms and profits.

#4755. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4754. Fortescue is using KUKA welding robots to handle 6 MW charging cables [video]

Humanoid robots aren’t ready to juice up the massive, 240-tonne electric haul trucks Fortescue is putting to work in Australia’s punishing Pilbara. Instead, the company is using specially modified and massively powerful automotive assembly-line robots from KUKA to wrangle the massive cables needed to deliver a mind-bending 6 MW of power to its trucks’ batteries.

While Chinese car brands capable of 2 MW “flash charging” are making headlines these days, Fortescue and Liebherr have been quietly working together to develop a 6MW charging system for their massive, ultra heavy-duty mining rigs since 2024 – but details about how the process actually works have been scarce.

Until now, that is. In a new video released by the company earlier this month, Fortescue explains how it delivers what amounts a controlled lightning bolt into the battery of its specially developed, 264 (short) ton Liebherr T264E electric haul truck. And, because the massive, liquid-cooled copper cables are too big, too heavy, and too dangerous for any human to handle, of course they’re using robots to get the job done.

“The challenge with a six megawatt charger is that nobody makes these, and therefore nobody makes a lot of the components, either,” says a Fortescue representative, in the video. “So, we’ve had to take systems and subsystems from different industries were using industrial robots that would normally be used for welding in a car factory.”

Fortescue was able to develop and refine its KUKA robots with help from a $10 million (AUD) grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), which were earmarked to help the company develop a six megawatt (MW) fast charger test unit and support its ultimate goal of achieving true net zero operations by 2030.

“Leveraging our world-class capability in battery and charging solutions from motorsport, the fast chargers have been developed for the challenging conditions of the Pilbara,” explained Fortescue Zero’s then-Chief Executive Officer, Ellie Coates, when the grant was announced in 2024. “Equipped with robotic connection options, they will be able to power Fortescue’s future 240-tonne Liebherr T 264 battery electric trucks in just 30 minutes.”

No need to reinvent the wheel, Cruise ship and other large vessels have ben using shore power for years when docked. these typical range from 7 MW to 16 MW, just borrow their tech, a overhead crane to lift the cable and an operator to plug it on

The Liebherr T264E packs an impossibly large 3.2 MWh (3,200 kWh) battery pack – the equivalent capacity of about 40 road-going Tesla Model Y crossovers – to put that 30 minute spec into context. You can check out the company’s official video, below, then let us know what you think of the 6 MW charging robots in the comments.

#4753. Kia’s EV6 GT beat out the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 in a German EV comparison test

Kia’s electric sports car beat out the Tesla Model Y Performance and BYD’s Sealion 7 in a recent comparison test by the German magazine Auto Motor und Sport, ranking first overall.

It wasn’t a German brand or a Chinese one. It wasn’t even the Tesla Model Y Performance. Kia’s electric sports car, the EV6 GT, took first place in a recent high-performance EV test in Germany, the heart of Europe.

The comparison test, held by German auto magazine Auto Motor und Sport, evaluated five high-performance EVs across seven categories: body, safety, comfort and convenience, powertrain, driving performance, environmental friendliness, and running costs.

The EV6 GT ranked first overall with 585 points, 9 points ahead of the Tesla Model Y Performance, which took second with 576 points.

The Zeekr 7GT ranked third with 569 points, followed by the Polestar 4 Coupe Dual Motor with 531 points, and the BYD Sealion 7 AWD Excellence, which ranked fifth with 508 points.

Kia’s electric sports car took the top spot in three of the seven categories: safety, powertrain, and driving performance. In the safety category, the EV6 GT scored highest for its superior braking and high-speed stability.

The EV6 GT earned praise in the powertrain category, boasting up to 650 horsepower and 770 Nm of torque from its dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain.

In the driving performance category, Kia’s electric sports car scored 20 points higher (96 points) than the Tesla Model Y Performance in second (76 points).

According to Auto Motor und Sport, the Kia EV6 GT took first place overall in the comparison test due to its “outstanding driving performance.”

Performance is one thing, but it also stands out with fun features, including Virtual Gear Shift. Borrowed from the Hyundai IONIQ 5 N, the feature simulates the feeling and sounds of a six-speed paddle-operated transmission.

Kia overhauled the interior for the newest model with its new connected car Navigation Cockpit (ccNC) infotainment system.

The new system includes dual 12.3″ navigation and driver display screens in a curved panoramic setup.

Kia’s electric sports car can sprint from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds. It uses a new 84 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

With 800V fast-charging capabilities, the Kia EV6 GT can recharge from 10% to 80% in as little as 18 minutes.

In Germany, the new Kia EV6 GT starts at 69,990 euros ($78,000). The Tesla Model Y Performance, on the other hand, starts at 63,970 euros in Germany. It offers a WLTP range of up to 360 miles (580 km) and accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds.

Which high-performance EV would you drive? The Kia EV6 GT or the Tesla Model Y Performance? Let us know in the comments.

Unfortunately, Kia said it was discontinuing the EV6 GT in the US “until further notice” earlier this year.

#4752. Matt Damon and David Letterman Pop into The Gilded Age Just for Funzies

HBO’s period drama got a very modern surprise from two very recognizable faces.

IF YOU’RE NOT familiar with HBO’s The Gilded Age, it’s a pretty easy show to explain. Set in New York City during the titular era—the rapidly changing 1880s—the show is an exploration of the rich-people trials and tribulations of a new money family (led by Carrie Coon and Morgan “Train Daddy” Spector) and their neighbors, an old money family (led by Christine Baranski).

One of the show’s most important aspects is its production design, with intricately built sets and elaborately planned costumes helping to transport its viewers back nearly 150 years. Immersion is the name of the game.

With a setup like that, The Gilded Age is just about the last show where you’d expect to see a couple of our most recognizable modern stars walk directly across the screen—but that’s just what Matt Damon and David Letterman did, less than 10 minutes into the show’s season 4 premiere.

Damon, the Oscar-winning movie star who earlier this year led Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Netflix’s The Rip, and Letterman, the legendary talk show host, walked across the screen in full costume, saying nothing, in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment.

As it turns out, according to a story published by Vulture, the whole thing was born from Letterman’s lifelong desire to make a surprise appearance in something as a background actor, something that began way back in 1977 when he saw a fellow comedian friend slyly appear in the background of a scene in Annie Hall.

In recent years, Letterman has apparently come close to shooting background scenes in Wes Anderson’s The Phoenician Scheme, the upcoming Michael B. Jordan-directed version of The Thomas Crown Affair, and Black Rabbit alongside Jason Bateman—but for one reason or another, none of them came to be.

Letterman filmed an upcoming episode of his current show, the Netflix interview series My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman, with Damon, and discovered that Damon and Ben Affleck began their careers as background actors, and, for the sake of the bit, figured this would be the perfect opportunity to see his dream come to fruition. “We thought, Okay, this could be the perfect opportunity,” Next Guest showrunner Isabel Richardson explained to Vulture. “It’d be really fun for Dave to do this with Academy Award–winner Matt Damon, and it tied into his origin story really well.”

Damon, luckily, was into the idea too—and they made it happen. “It was a kind of hysterical moment when our production supervisor Leah Baker came up to me on set and was like, ‘Well, I have a kind of funny, interesting question: Would you like Dave Letterman and Matt Damon to be background on our set one day?’” Gilded Age showrunner Churchill said in the same Vulture story. “I just started laughing.”

Surprise appearances and cameos have long been a part of Damon’s playbook. Marvel fans certainly remember his brief appearances in movies like Deadpool 2 and Thor: Ragnarok, while fans of Damon’s frequent collaborator Steven Soderbergh’s movies won’t forget his surprise turns in movies like No Sudden Move and Che: Part Two. He even appeared in a very brief role in Ethan Coen’s Drive Away Dolls after working with Ethan and his brother Joel on the 2010 hit True Grit.

Perhaps Damon’s most memorable (and truly most random) cameo comes in the 2004 comedy Eurotrip, though. He appears early in the film as Donnie, the lead singer of an alt-rock band who sings a song about the affair he was apparently having with the main character’s girlfriend. “Scotty Doesn’t Know” is a pillar of both 2000s pop-punk and that era’s teen sex comedy movement, and Damon’s completely out-of-nowhere cameo is a huge reason why.

And, look, HBO seems to enjoy this kind of thing anyway. Just last month, we spotted the University of Nebraska’s head football coach Matt Rhule in the final episode of Lanterns. Does his appearance make sense in a show set in Nebraska? Sure. Did we ever expect to see Matt Rhule in an acclaimed, highly watched HBO drama set in a superhero world? No, we certainly did not.

It’s fun (and probably a bit trippy at first) to come to grips with seeing who you think you’re seeing. And if, somehow, you don’t know who either of those two are, you probably won’t notice at all and won’t think a thing. And isn’t that how all great cameos should go, really?

#4751. New Jersey may finally reverse its draconian e-bike law after massive backlash

New Jersey lawmakers are already looking to walk back one of the country’s most controversial e-bike laws, just months after the sweeping new regulations took effect and sparked widespread backlash from riders, bicycle shops, and advocacy groups.

A newly introduced bill, S4830, sponsored by State Senator Raj Mukherji, would remove licensing, registration, and insurance requirements for low-speed electric bicycles with motors rated at 750W or less and a maximum motor-powered speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). This includes Class 1 and Class 2 electric bicycles.

The proposal would essentially restore bicycle-like treatment for these two classes of e-bikes, importantly including throttle-equipped models that make up the majority of e-bikes sold in the state and more broadly in the US, while maintaining stricter requirements for faster and more powerful electric bicycles.

The move comes after New Jersey’s previous governor, Phil Murphy, signed a sweeping e-bike law in January following several tragic crashes involving young riders.

That legislation, which took full effect in July, eliminated the state’s previous three-class e-bike framework and introduced licensing and registration requirements for all electric bicycles, including ordinary low-speed commuter models. Throttle-equipped and faster e-bikes also faced insurance requirements.

As we previously reported, New Jersey bicycle shops experienced devastating sales declines after the law took effect, with some reporting drops of 20% to 90%. Several businesses were forced to lay off employees, downsize, or even close entirely as e-bike sales and usage plummeted.

Meanwhile, riders faced confusing new requirements that made e-bikes considerably less accessible, which was particularly impactful for lower-income residents, people with disabilities, and those who rely on electric bicycles for daily transportation.

I own a Class 3 e-bike, but I also acknowledge that with its potential assisted speed of 28mph it's of a different breed than Class 1/2 bikes -- that's just too fast in crowded bike lanes or shared use paths.

The first priority should be to target reckless riding by anyone, and illegal bikes should be confiscated if they're involved.

The original law was intended to improve safety, but critics argued that it largely punished responsible riders instead of addressing the growing problem of high-powered electric motorcycles masquerading as bicycles. Only responsible riders actually registered their bikes as required by law, while others were deterred from cycling, and the hooligan riders who often gave e-bikes a bad name continued to ride illegally.

After all, requiring someone riding a 20 mph (32 km/h) commuter e-bike to obtain a driver’s license and register their bicycle does little to address reckless riding on machines capable of highway speeds.

The newly proposed legislation appears to acknowledge that distinction, offering a more targeted approach that could preserve reasonable safety regulations without making ordinary e-bike ownership unnecessarily complicated.

S4830 still needs to work its way through the legislature before becoming law, but for New Jersey’s struggling e-bike industry, it’s a promising sign that lawmakers may finally be listening. It is still widely argued that requiring electric bicycles from 21-28 mph (32-45 km/h) to require a driver’s license and registration is overly burdensome, but at least the state appears to be moving back toward the right direction.

#4750. Tesla pushes Optimus deliveries to late 2027, says hands still a problem

Elon Musk now says Tesla will start delivering Optimus humanoid robots to outside customers around the end of 2027. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call, he said the hands, the robot’s durability and its AI all still need work before then.

Those are the same three problems every humanoid robot company is fighting. And despite Musk’s claim that nobody is close to Tesla, XPeng and Hyundai’s Boston Dynamics look at least as far along.

Musk said Tesla has started early production of Optimus on its high-volume line in Fremont, where Model S and Model X used to be built. Most of a line designed for a million robots a year is installed, but he said it will take at least a year, possibly longer, to reach that rate of about 20,000 units a week, because parts of the design are still changing.

He listed what has to be solved first: the AI, the electromechanical design, and reliability, including making sure the robot doesn’t wear out after a month of use. He expects those issues to be solved around the end of next year. That’s when Tesla expects to deliver Optimus to companies outside Tesla, starting with industrial jobs that are dangerous, repetitive or need to run around the clock.

When an analyst asked where the design was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the hand as one of the hardest hardware areas, along with custom gears that still carry reliability concerns. Musk agreed the hand is the main issue, explaining that fingers need to be soft enough to handle delicate objects while surviving constant wear, and robots can’t heal like human skin can.

On the AI side, Musk said Tesla is still working through problems with the AI architecture. Tesla doesn’t have a fleet of robots collecting data the way its cars do for FSD, so it plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots and have them practice tasks in what it calls an Optimus Academy. Tesla also plans to put its AI5 chip in Optimus around April 2027.

Musk also promised an Optimus video within a month or two showing the robot doing tasks that aren’t pre-programmed. He argued that many humanoid demos look impressive but only run scripted routines that wouldn’t hold up in the real world.

None of this is new. Last month, we reported that Tesla had ramped Optimus to hundreds of units a week, but that the robots couldn’t generalize to new tasks. According to The Information, the hand and forearm had over 100 small parts assembled by hand, touch sensors had reliability issues, and the AI could take days to learn basic tasks.

Tesla’s own Q3 shareholder letter now calls the bots coming off the Fremont line “the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured.” So every Optimus before this quarter wasn’t production quality.

And the timeline keeps moving. In 2024, Musk said Tesla would build Optimus for internal use in 2025 and hopefully in high volume for other companies in 2026. In January 2025, he said Tesla would build about 10,000 robots that year, with “several thousand” doing useful work by year-end. He later admitted none were. Now external deliveries are a late-2027 target.

Musk said on the call that, to the best of his knowledge, “there is no one that is even close to Tesla” on a general-purpose humanoid robot. That’s hard to square with what competitors have shown.

XPeng turned on an automated IRON production line in Guangzhou in September, with more than 80% of core processes automated. IRON has 21 degrees of freedom in each hand and runs XPeng’s physical AI model on three in-house Turing chips. XPeng plans mass production by the end of 2026, deliveries in the first half of 2027 starting with stores and malls, and a European rollout in the second half of 2027. That’s a similar timeline to Tesla’s, if not slightly ahead.

XPeng is dealing with the same reality. It hasn’t shipped IRON to a paying customer, and its timelines have slipped like everyone else’s.

Boston Dynamics started producing its electric Atlas in January and says all of its 2026 Atlas deployments are already committed, including to Google DeepMind, whose AI models Boston Dynamics is integrating. In September, it opened a robot training center at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia, where Atlas is learning to sequence car parts for the assembly line. Hyundai plans to deploy 25,000 robots across its plants over the next few years. Boston Dynamics also hired Milan Kovac, Tesla’s former head of Optimus, in January.

Boston Dynamics also seems to have taken a more pragmatic approach to hands, prioritizing sturdy grippers for industrial parts over human-like dexterity. That’s less impressive in a demo, but it’s a way around the problem Tesla says is holding it back.

My prediction is that Optimus will forever be delayed. It's like FSD in Tesla cars -- never quite good enough to really take off and always one or two releases away from fixing everything. At least a Tesla car with a broken FSD is still a good car. Optimus with a bad brain is an interesting-looking boat anchor.

Tesla is facing the exact same problems as everyone else: hands that survive real work, robots reliable enough to pay for themselves, and AI that can handle tasks it wasn’t trained for. Nobody has cracked generalization yet, Tesla included. The difference is that Tesla’s competitors aren’t telling investors they have no competition.

Based on what’s public, XPeng has a more automated production line and a similar delivery date, and Boston Dynamics is already deploying Atlas in a car factory with committed customers. Tesla may well have the most robots built, but building robots isn’t the hard part. Making them useful is.

Tesla has promised a video in a month or two. If it shows Optimus doing real, unscripted work, great. But we’ve heard about Optimus timelines before, and they’ve slipped every year. Why should late 2027 be different?

#4748. Why We Can’t Just Stop Feeling Guilty

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

It’s something I come across in the consulting room all the time. A client has come to therapy to stop doing something she knows is not serving her. “I need to stop taking her calls”; “I need to stop always picking up after him”; “I need to stop neglecting myself.” So what gets in the way? This is a question I ask a lot. And more often than not, the answer is guilt: “I just feel too guilty when I don’t do it.” And after some probing, the story often goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. I’m not who I want to be. If I got rid of my guilt, I wouldn’t know who I am anymore. I’m always the one who takes care of others and fixes things. What if I let go of my guilt and I become lazy and selfish?

I’ve changed my approach to guilt in therapy, and it’s still evolving, but It’s at this point that I used to fall back onto my trusted therapy tools. If this is a belief that is not serving my client, the next logical step is to find a way to challenge it. The problem is that most of my clients know that logically, rationally, they need to stop taking care of everyone else. They know that they need to set boundaries. They even know that they are not, in fact, selfish or lazy because they have mountains of evidence to the contrary.

So why can you not just stop feeling guilty? The question is, in many ways, as nonsensical as asking why we cannot stop feeling anxious or sad or angry. Yet somehow, we have constructed this idea in popular psychology that guilt is something inconvenient we need to let go of. What if we start by trying to understand why you might feel guilty in the first place? Just as anxiety is an emotion that we can never seem to get rid of, it might be that feeling guilty serves a function in our lives that we need to understand. Only then can we find ways to accept that this uncomfortable feeling is unavoidable but does not need to define who we are.

Guilt in itself is what researchers have called a “prosocial” emotion—that is to say, guilt will often motivate us to repair relationships when we have done something wrong. In its purest form, guilt supports cooperation in our social groups. But, just like anxiety can spiral out of control, overinflated guilt that stops us from looking after ourselves has moved far beyond its prosocial utility.

What makes guilt spiral out of control? Researchers suggest that what my clients might be suffering from is “omnipotent responsibility guilt.” The origins of this particular type of guilt feeling can be traced back to our earliest relationships. If a child grows up in a relationship with a parent who is unpredictable or whose feelings are uncontained, the child can learn that it is safer to take responsibility for the adult’s feelings and try to fix them. Children are in a precariously vulnerable state—dependent on their caregiver for safety, regardless of how emotionally safe that caregiver might be.

To keep that caregiver safe in the child’s mind, it can be easier to construct an internal model in which the responsibility for the parent’s happiness is with the child, and the child is to blame if the parent is unhappy. The child continuously fears and predicts relational rupture, and that prediction model grows into adulthood, where it becomes the foundation of an identity in which everyone else’s feelings are more important than our own, and we feel selfish for looking after ourselves.

So, what my therapy tools did not take into consideration, then, is that guilt can be linked to a deep sense of relational danger. Because the story, in fact, goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. But if it’s my fault, at least that means I can make it better. And that feels a lot safer than the alternative. Because if I’m not the one who has done something wrong, that means the ones who were meant to keep me safe might not be safe after all. And then the whole world stops being safe.

It can be difficult to make the leap from our present feelings of guilt to our earliest experiences. But the intensity with which many of my clients hold on to their guilt suggests that it fulfills a deep function that feels like survival. By the time we are adults, a tendency to accept responsibility for others’ feelings may have become fiercely intertwined with who we believe we are. We protect ourselves by telling ourselves we are lazy or selfish when we veer off course because, for many of my clients, guilt has become the thing that keeps their relationships, and with that their sense of self, alive.

Tracing this back opens the doors to new therapy tools that can slowly address the impasse so many of my clients can find themselves in:

The reason we cannot just stop feeling guilty is because our feelings are there for a reason. We may not objectively have done anything wrong, but our guilt feelings might still serve a function, even an outdated one that nevertheless keeps us feeling safe. Remember that it is OK to set boundaries, and it is also OK to find it hard. Be kind to yourself and don’t embark on this by yourself. We are social beings who learn safety in relationship, and we need each other’s company to do that.

#4747. Scania speeds up switch to silent semi trucks with Chinese production

Record fuel prices driven by the dumb oil war in Iran are fueling a faster-than-expected switch to electric trucks in the world’s biggest freight markets – and Swedish heavy truck brand Scania is scrambling to meet demand with a new factory in China.

The Swedish truck maker is set to begin manufacturing battery-powered trucks at its new Rugao assembly plant in China as soon as it receives a license, according to Scania Chief Executive Officer Christian Levin.

In an interview given in Södertälje, Levin said he expects electric trucks to account for half of China’s market by the start of 2027. “We have had to speed up those plans,” Levin explained. “It’s always quite a complicated process in China to get licenses to do different things, but I have to say: it has moved much faster than we could have imagined.”

Chinese electric semi truck sales jumped almost 80% in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025, and are on pace to account for over 30% of all heavy trucks sold this year – and that pace is accelerating.

Scania built the Rugao plant last year, making it the Traton Group’s first wholly-owned factory in China. The facility will serve China and other Asian markets, and can build both conventional diesel and battery-powered trucks on the same assembly lines.

“It is happening quickly and that’s incredibly fascinating,” says Levin. “It means they have found a way to expand charging infrastructure and the power grid, which is the biggest challenge we have in many countries around the world, including Europe.”

I would respond to that by saying that China has a political system that makes the betterment of society as-a-whole a higher priority than corporate profits and creating shareholder value, but nobody asked me and this isn’t one of those blogs. #4746. Volkswagen is launching its most affordable EV yet in 2027, starting at around €20,000

Volkswagen’s upcoming electric car will be smaller and lower-priced than the ID. Polo, starting at around €20,000 ($22,500).

The new Electric Urban Car Family is the Volkswagen Group’s answer to Chinese automakers like BYD: a new lineup of compact, entry-level electric cars.

The lineup currently includes the Volkswagen ID. Polo, ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the same MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced base versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to introduce an even smaller, more affordable EV in 2027.

Volkswagen revealed the ID. EVERY1 concept car last March, a preview of its upcoming entry-level EV that will arrive in 2027 starting at around €20,000.

The ID. EVERY1, which is expected to go on sale as the ID. Up! next year, is “the last piece of the puzzle,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said, as it aims to offer the widest selection in the volume segment.

With a length of 3,880 mm, the entry-level EV is positioned between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Although that is tiny, VW said it will offer space for four passengers and a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

Volkswagen has yet to reveal details, but the €20,000 EV is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery as the base ID. Polo and ID. Cross to keep costs down.

The ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery has a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller model will likely offer around the same or slightly more range.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen delivered on its promise to launch the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery for under €25,000. Will it do the same with the new entry-level model at around €20,000? We will find out shortly.

It will be produced in Portugal, this has been confirmed ages ago.

According to Spanish auto magazine Autofácil, Volkswagen could manufacture the €20,000 EV in Spain, although Volkswagen has yet to confirm a production site.

The Group currently produces the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval at its Martorell plant, while the ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq are manufactured at the Navarra plant, both in Spain.

Volkswagen’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a promising start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

While those in the US will miss out on the new entry-level EV, Volkswagen is launching the ID. Tiguan in 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

Kia is betting its new lineup of affordable EVs, like the EV3, can beat the incoming wave of Chinese models in Canada, but affordability is only one part of the equation.

After launching the EV3 in Canada in August, Kia said it was the lowest-priced electric vehicle on the market, starting at CAD $39,744.

It may not hold the title for long, though. Canada struck a deal with China earlier this year, allowing up to 49,000 electric vehicles to enter the Canadian market at a 6.1% tariff rate.

According to Kia Canada’s COO, Elias El-Achhab, the company sees the deal’s timing as an opportunity.

“I thought it was just a bonus,” El-Achhab said during Automotive News Canada’s Retail Forum this week.

Kia is “trying to be the first affordable EV brand in the country,” he said, but that doesn’t necessarily mean just offering the lowest-priced vehicle. The Korean automaker is focusing on offering EVs at an affordable price that still come with the tech and features buyers want.

The EV3 (check out our review) joins Kia’s other mass-market electric vehicles, including the EV4 and EV5, that are now on sale in Canada.

When asked whether Kia could face more competition from China because of its positioning as a low-cost brand, El-Achhab said: “I actually think the opposite.”
