#4742. The Psychological Origins of Fear-Based Advertising

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

When I was an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins University, I heard the story about how John B. Watson, a psychologist who is considered the father of the classical conditioning strand of American behaviorism (a term that he coined), was fired from a tenure-track position for having a sexual relationship with his 21-year-old graduate assistant, Rosalie Rayner. An earlier example of a very esteemed scholar who was fired by Hopkins for similar prurient reasons (in both cases they later married their girlfriends after becoming divorced from their first wives) involved the great philosopher, mathematician, and logician Charles Sanders Peirce. Neither man ever attained another academic post. While Watson went on to have great success outside of academia, Peirce continued as an independent scholar who lived in abject poverty, relying on financial support from many admirers, most notably his former JHU doctoral student William James, considered the father of American psychology and the co-developer, with Peirce, of the philosophical school of pragmatism.

The 1920 experiment for which Watson, assisted by Rayner, became famous (a year before they fired him, Hopkins doubled his salary in an attempt to keep him from leaving) involved an infant later known as “Little Albert.” The experiment exposed Albert, at age nine months, to various neutral stimuli–including a white rat, monkeys, and dogs–thus demonstrating his absence of fear. At age 11 months, every time that Albert reached for the white rat, a scary, loud noise (Watson striking a steel bar with a hammer behind the child’s head) occurred. The result was that the infant developed a fear response (distress and crying) to the rat even in the absence of the noise. This fear response generalized to other white objects, including cotton wool, a fur coat, and a Santa Claus mask with a white beard. Watson planned to extinguish the fear through exposure, but the experiment (today considered profoundly unethical) was prematurely ended by the child’s mother. Their scientific claim was that classical conditioning could be used to establish emotional responses, especially fear, in children.

In 1928, Watson and Rayner (who went on to have two children together) co-authored a child-rearing book, “Psychological Care of Infant and Child” in which they used the results of their experiment to argue (based on zero evidence) that a child’s personality is formed entirely by environmental forces with no role for innate nature or instincts. The book’s most controversial–and, to me, horrifying–advice for parents was that they should not hug, kiss, or show affection to their children, in order to toughen them up for the grim world they would face as adults. Interestingly, Watson and Rayner had two sons, both raised according to their no-love method. As adults, both attempted suicide, one of them successfully. (A third adult child, a daughter from Watson’s first marriage, also attempted suicide, and blamed it, whether fairly or not, on her father).

After being forced out of academia, Watson was hired by the New York-based advertising company J. Walter Thompson. He thrived there, eventually becoming a vice-president of the firm. The basis of Watson’s success as an ad man was developing the idea, based on his view of behaviorism, that the key to persuading consumers to buy a particular product was conditioning them to the idea that by not buying it they were exposing themselves or their loved ones to a feared physical or social danger. In the physical realm, Watson persuaded consumers to buy Scott’s toilet paper by showing doctors grimly surrounding a patient whose medical condition was attributed to wiping their bum with “harsh toilet tissue.” Another ad campaign, on behalf of the Johnson & Johnson company, emphasized to mothers that they were exposing their children to dread diseases by not purchasing the company’s hygiene products. But fear was also used as the basis for Watson’s ads in the social domain, with one example involving buying a brand of toothpaste not to promote good dental health but to avoid the social rejection that supposedly flows from bad breath and discolored teeth.

Watson thus pioneered in America the use of psychological concepts as the basis for advertising campaigns, grounding it on the conditioning of emotional responses, particularly fear. He was followed in the related field of public relations by Edward Bernays, a double nephew of Sigmund Freud (his mother was Freud’s sister and his father was the brother of Freud’s wife), and who based his ideas of propaganda–the title of his most famous book–not on behaviorism but, very loosely, on psychoanalytic theory. Bernays, whose parents moved from Austria to the US when he was an infant, often visited his uncle (who gifted him Cuban cigars, perhaps in thanks for getting one of his books published in America) and was a pioneer in the field of public relations. Although not himself trained as a psychoanalyst, Bernays claimed to have developed a public relations theory based on his famous uncle’s notion that people’s actions are controlled less by conscious ideas than by unconscious desires and fears.

Bernays, like Watson, was successful in promoting commercial products, with his biggest success, influenced by advice from Freud’s translator A.A. Brill, occurring on behalf of the American Tobacco Company. The purpose of that campaign was to persuade women to overcome the taboo against female smoking by portraying Lucky Strike cigarettes as phallic symbols empowering women to escape from male oppression. Bernays’ efforts, however, were mainly in the public sector, and involved such activities as drumming up support for America’s entry into WWI. Years later, when working for the United Fruit Company, Bernays promoted the CIA-led overthrow of the left-leaning President of Guatemala, Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán. In that campaign, Bernays took a page from the John B. Watson playbook by portraying Arbenz as a communist who posed a threat to the U.S. and its people. Bernays later followed the same Red-Scare playbook in the early days of the Vietnam War, but later backed off from the effort when that war became unwinnable, both in the field and in the realm of public opinion.

Bernays justified his efforts at propaganda (a term he stopped using when it began to take on negative connotations) by claiming that it was essential in a democracy for its leaders to have a way to keep the populace from spiraling out of control. Although Watson did not address the role of advertising in a democracy, he shared with Bernays the idea that people’s actions are governed mainly by emotion, and that psychology provided emotion-based mechanisms of social control. Neither Watson nor Bernays showed any concern about the need to base their arguments on actual truth. Ominous implications for the future of democracy in the U.S. and other countries flow from the ubiquity of political advertising based on fear-mongering that in many cases is based on completely made-up facts. It is in the political arena, more than in his dangerous advice to parents, that the lessons from John B. Watson’s Little Albert experiment have come to have profound influence on public life.

#4741. Ferrari Luce EV starts at $560,800 in the US, $80K less than expected

Ferrari’s first electric car, the Luce, will start at $560,800 in the US, with American deliveries planned for the second quarter of 2027. Car and Driver first reported the figure, and Ferrari has confirmed it.

That’s roughly $80,000 under the ~$640,000 number that has followed the Luce since its unveiling in May, including in our own coverage. But Americans aren’t getting a deal.

Ferrari didn’t give a US price when it launched the Luce in Rome on May 25. It gave a European one: €550,000. Most outlets, us included, ran that through the exchange rate of the day, about $1.16 per euro, and got to roughly $640,000.

The problem is that European car prices are normally quoted with VAT included, and Italy’s rate is 22%.

Take the tax out and the Luce costs about €450,800 in Italy. At today’s rate of roughly $1.12 per euro, that’s around $506,000. So the US price is about $55,000 higher than what an Italian buyer pays before taxes, and American buyers still owe state sales tax on top of the $560,800.

Some of that gap is trade policy. European-built cars now face a 15% US tariff, and Ferrari already raised prices on part of its US lineup last year to cover it. The $560,800 also doesn’t include options, and Ferrari hasn’t published what those cost. Nobody buys a base Ferrari.

None of this will slow sales. Ferrari sold out its 2026 Luce allocation of just under 500 units in less than two months, with China doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In August, the first production chassis went for $40 million at a charity auction for the Ferrari Foundation.

That’s despite a rough reveal. The design, done with Jony Ive and Marc Newson’s LoveFrom, got hammered online, and Ferrari’s stock dropped sharply in the days after the launch before recovering.

The hardware is serious. The Luce uses four motors, one per wheel, for 1,035 hp combined. It’s built on an 800V architecture with a 122 kWh battery pack from SK On, charges at up to 350 kW, and Ferrari rates it at 529 km (329 miles) WLTP. It does 0-100 km/h in 2.5 seconds and weighs 2,260 kg (4,982 lb). It’s also Ferrari’s first five-seater.

For comparison, a Lucid Air Sapphire with over 1,200 hp costs around $250,000. You could buy two and still have change left over.

"None of this will slow sales. Ferrari sold out its 2026 Luce allocation of just under 500 units in less than two months, with China doing a lot of the heavy lifting."

This only proves that the world has too many mega wealthy people with more money than brains. All while the middle class continues to shrink and more people are headed towards homelessness.

The bigger story is that the price clearly doesn’t matter to Ferrari’s buyers. Plenty of luxury brands have convinced themselves that wealthy buyers won’t pay supercar money for an electric car. Maserati killed the electric MC20 Folgore over exactly that fear. Ferrari just put a $560,800 sticker on a four-door EV with a polarizing design and sold out a year of production anyway.

We’re not convinced every one of those orders comes from love of the car. Ferrari’s allocation game rewards loyal customers, and some buyers are surely taking a Luce to stay in line for the next limited-run V12. But a deposit is a deposit.

The real test comes in 2027 and 2028, once the first wave of collectors has its cars and the Luce has to sell on its own merits. Will it?Personally, I hope that the Luce leads to Ferrari trying to make some electric sports cars.

#4740. Job Crafting at 25

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Twenty-five years ago, Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton published a paper that asked readers to look at work a little bit differently. Rather than viewing jobs as something organizations designed and employees simply carried out, they argued that employees could reshape their work in ways that make it more meaningful, engaging, and sustainable. They called the process job crafting.

I recently spent several days sifting through two special issues of the Journal of Business and Psychology, 41(3) and 41(4), marking the 25th anniversary. Together, they contain 19 papers. Individually, each paper tackles a fairly specific question. Collectively, though, they tell a much bigger story. I've whittled that bigger story down to three takeaways that really stood out to me.

The first thing that struck me was how much the questions have evolved over 25 years.

The original paper introduced job crafting as a new way of thinking about work. Unsurprisingly, much of the early research focused on understanding whether job crafting was associated with outcomes like engagement, well-being, performance, and job satisfaction. That was an important first step. Researchers first needed to establish what job crafting was, how it could be measured, and whether it was linked to meaningful workplace outcomes.

Reading these special issues, though, it became clear that the conversation has moved forward. Very few papers were still asking whether job crafting was generally associated with positive outcomes (we’ve established that), and the ones that did were mostly examining the issue through the lens of contextual factors. Instead, researchers were asking much more specific questions about how the process actually unfolds.

For example, Parker et al. (2026) examined whether the relationship between work characteristics and job crafting is reciprocal rather than one-directional, arguing that employees shape their jobs while their jobs simultaneously shape their opportunities to craft. Another, Rudolph et al. (2026), explored whether the effects of autonomy and workload follow nonlinear patterns, suggesting that too little or too much of either may actually reduce employees' ability to craft their work.

Other papers asked equally nuanced questions. Does job crafting operate differently for younger and older employees (Schepp & Boehm, 2026)? What role does job crafting play for interns transitioning into the workforce (Kim et al., 2026)? How might employees with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder use job crafting to better align their work with their strengths and challenges (Weinhardt et al., 2026)?

The broader message from all these papers is that there doesn't appear to be a single formula for effective job crafting. What works depends on the person, the job, and the situation. That may not sound particularly exciting, but I actually see it as a sign that this research domain has matured. Once researchers become reasonably confident that an idea is important, they start asking more interesting questions about how people can make it work. After 25 years, job crafting research seems to have reached that point.

The second thing that struck me was how much the idea itself has expanded.

The original paper described three broad ways employees could craft their work: by changing the tasks they performed, the relationships they developed, and the way they thought about their jobs. Twenty-five years later, researchers are applying that same basic idea in a variety of new directions.

These special issues included papers on career crafting, which extends the concept beyond one's current job to the broader arc of a person's career (Li et al., 2026); team job crafting, which examines how groups of employees collectively reshape their work (Wang et al., 2026); and time-spatial job crafting, which explores how employees intentionally structure where and when they work in hybrid environments (Demerouti, 2026). The introductory article also positioned playful work design in the same context as job crafting, another bottom-up approach to proactively shaping work (Bakker & Slemp, 2026).

None of those ideas felt like a stretch to me. In fact, they all seem to build naturally on the original insight that employees aren't simply passive recipients of the jobs organizations create. Instead, they can actively shape their own work experiences.

What I found most interesting wasn't any single extension. It was realizing how pliable the original idea has proven to be. Twenty-five years later, researchers are still finding new ways to apply the basic insight that employees don't simply have to adapt to work—they can actively shape it. More importantly, that insight is no longer confined to an individual employee crafting an individual job.

The third thing that stood out to me was how much more nuanced the conversation has become. Early job crafting research often focused on demonstrating that employees who crafted their jobs tended to experience better outcomes. The anniversary papers paint a more complicated picture. They increasingly ask when job crafting helps, when it doesn't, and what factors influence whether it succeeds.

For example, Rudolph and colleagues argued that more job crafting isn't necessarily better. Like many workplace behaviors, there may be a point where additional crafting provides diminishing returns or even becomes counterproductive. Additionally, Parker and colleagues suggested that the relationship between job crafting and positive work outcomes may not simply run in one direction. Rather than job crafting causing engagement or well-being, employees who are already engaged or thriving may also be more likely to craft their jobs, creating an ongoing cycle of mutual influence.

Other papers highlight the importance of context. Schepp and Boehm explored how job crafting changes across the lifespan, suggesting that what works for a younger employee may not be the same as what works later in a career. Weinhardt and colleagues examined how ADHD shapes job crafting, reminding us that individual differences matter as well.

To me, this is perhaps the most important evolution. Rather than treating job crafting as a universally beneficial phenomenon, these papers recognize that its effects depend on the circumstances. That's ultimately a much more useful way to think about job crafting because it shifts the focus from encouraging more crafting to understanding what kind of crafting is likely to help, for whom, and under what conditions.

Reading through these special issues turned out to be far more interesting than I expected. Many of the papers were less about introducing new ideas than about taking stock of how job crafting has evolved over the past 25 years. That evolution resulted in researchers asking better questions, applying the concept in new contexts, and developing a more nuanced understanding of when job crafting actually helps.

If there's a practical lesson from all of this, it's that work is probably more flexible than we often assume—but not infinitely so. Most of us have at least some ability to shape how we experience our jobs. The trick, though, isn't simply to craft more. It's to understand which changes are actually likely to make work better for you in your particular role and circumstances.

#4737. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4736. How to turn your smartphone into a mobile video editing suite

Published Oct 24, 2026 8:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

With so many smartphone apps in the modern age locked (or partially locked) behind paywalls, it’s important to grab the free ones when they become available—and on rare occasions, it’s the biggest software companies on the planet offering apps free of charge. Adobe Premiere for iOS launched back in September 2025, and a year later, we got Adobe Premiere for Android too. You don’t need an Adobe account or a subscription to use these apps (unlike the desktop equivalents)—the only paid components are credits for AI image and video generation, if you want to use those tools.

With these apps available, there’s really no excuse for sharing sub-standard video. You get a wealth of editing features right on your mobile screen, all optimized to suit the smaller display and the more limited capabilities of a phone versus a full computer.

We’re going to concentrate on the Android app here, as it’s the one most recently launched, but the features are the same on the iPhone too. You can even use Premiere across multiple Android and iOS devices.

It’s easy enough to get started with Premiere: From the main screen, tap the + (plus) button to choose a saved video clip or image to use as the starting point for a new project, or select New blank project. Either will take you to the timeline view, and you can then use the + (plus) button on the timeline to load in more content.

The layout is going to be familiar if you’ve used a video editor before. Photos and videos make up the main timeline, and if you select them, you get handles around them—use these handles to shorten or lengthen the clips. Select a video on the timeline, then tap Split to cut it in two at the current playhead position (that’s wherever the long vertical white line is in the timeline).

Your video project is previewed above the timeline, and you can use the playback controls to go backward and forward through it. The other options you’ll see on the toolbar include Audio (for dropping in a voiceover or some stock music), Text (for titles and overlays), and Generate (for producing generative AI content). You can also select Files to load local files (such as audio snippets) from your phone.

Select anything on the timeline to get more options for it. For a video clip, these will include Retime (for changing the speed of a clip or freezing it), Filters (for adjusting the look of a clip), Effects (tweaks like glows or shakes), and tools to mirror, flip, or duplicate whatever you’ve got selected. To change transitions, tap on the borders between scenes.

Then there are the generative AI tools, which you can get to by tapping on the Generate button underneath the timeline. This part of the app requires an Adobe account—the account itself is free, but you’ll be restricted in terms of your AI usage before you have to start paying for credits.

If you want a quicker, easier way to make content, there are plenty of ready-made templates to use. You’ll see these on the front screen, under headings like Lifestyle and Beauty. Tap on a template to view it, then choose Use this template to start making it your own.

Making it your own means picking images and videos from your phone’s library to add to the template you just viewed. As you make your selections, you’ll see the template slots fill up underneath (you don’t have to use all of them)—when you’re done, choose Next to see the finished product.

This will have the same transitions, timings, titles, and audio as your template, and if you’re happy with that, then tap Export to send the video somewhere else. There are some basic editing tools here as well: Select one of the images or videos you’ve dropped in, and you can trim them or replace them with the buttons at the bottom.

To customize the clip even more, choose Full editor to return to the fully featured interface we looked at above, complete with filters, effects, and everything else. Note that once you’ve converted your template-based video to work with the full timeline interface, you can’t go back into template mode with the same project.

It’s an app that works well for quick video creations and more detailed projects you want to do on your phone, and you’ll also get numerous settings (resolution, frame rate, quality) when it’s time to export your work. If you do sign up for an Adobe account and pay for the Creative Cloud suite, you can easily sync your projects with Premiere on the desktop.

#4735. What if a Chatbot Really Could Be a Friend?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Co-authored by Ryan Moore, Ph.D., assistant professor, iSchool and School of Computing, the University of Texas at Austin.

My daughter bought me a label maker for my birthday. I had never considered using a label maker. But suddenly, the leftovers in the freezer required a name and a date, the file drawers in my office needed topic indicators, and the boxes with holiday decorations are now clearly marked with what is inside. Who knew that something you never had could be so indispensable?

Chatbots may be the label makers of the social world. We never knew how useful they could be until they arrived. A chatbot, especially when powered by today’s generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, can feel like talking with another person. With names like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, chatbots may play important and unique roles in our social lives.

New technologies present exciting opportunities, but also reasons to be cautious or concerned. These new AI tools usher in concerns about job obsolescence, security, and the environment. But when used appropriately, AI tools could enhance our social lives in meaningful ways. Let’s focus on enhancement here, not substitution.

I’ve mentioned previously that different types of social ties fulfill diverse social needs: belongingness, information, everyday tasks, support, intimacy, and feeling loved and cared for. No single social tie fulfills all needs. We benefit from a mix of romantic partners, children, friends, neighbors, close acquaintances (i.e., fringeships), and even strangers.

Historically, new technologies introduced possibilities for social interaction. For example, since the first part of the 20th century, when the telephone entered everyday life, we commonly talk with people who aren’t present.

Chatbots differ from technologies that facilitate communication between people. Chatbots can perform autonomous social functions when humans aren’t available. They provide individualized, tailored information; a sounding board to strengthen human relationships; a forum to think aloud without managing another human’s reactions; and they can reinforce decisions. Consistent affirmation has several limitations and could harm more than help us, but if the input is weighed for what it is, it can be supportive.

Why wouldn’t we want to add that to our social repertoire?

In the 1980s, L.L. Bean advertised a 24-hour retail service that you could call toll-free day or night. This was a novel approach, but it was limited to ordering fishing gear or a jacket.

Chatbots are available to discuss anything, anytime, anywhere. You can wake them at 2 a.m. when you are ruminating about a talk you have to give. And they have no expectations of reciprocity. There are hotlines available anytime, too (if you ever feel suicidal, call 988 to speak with a human—not a chatbot). But chatbots will shoot the breeze.

Other available software keeps a calendar. A chatbot goes a step further by solving problems, generating a schedule, and tailoring an agenda to your needs and priorities. Chatbots determine the information we need, then find it.

Chatbots may also support people with deficits. They can take notes during a class for a student with a learning disability. Someone in early-stage dementia can ask the chatbot the same question repeatedly, without taxing a caregiver.

Chatbots can help with tasks that require detail or repetition. It can tutor a third grader in multiplication tables over and over and never needs to go fix dinner. It can format or update a spreadsheet and quickly pull information from the web. Human effort may be better spent on the complex steps in each project.

Counterintuitively, Chatbots could enhance our human relationships. Communication between people can benefit from input that balances what you want with predictions of another person’s reactions. Chatbots offer:

In 2000, a search engine called Google spread widely, accessing a universe of information. The website even became a verb. I googled, “the year Google became popular” to land on 2000.

But chatbots can personalize information. With the prompt: “I want a vacation that balances sites, hiking, and great food,” ChatGPT suggested Tucson, Arizona. Over time, the chatbot remembers my preferences.

It has pulled recipes (simple, pescatarian), recommended books, and culled my movie recommendations. No one crafts your personal time the way your chatbot can in minutes.

Any particular relationship comes with constraints. You don’t hug your customers. You don’t send memos to your grandma. Chatbots are additions to our social networks, but limitations make them tools rather than social partners.

Chatbot advice can be harmful on important issues, including finance or health. Issues of consequence require human research and input; chatbots have led people severely astray.

Researchers have identified addictive or compulsive engagement, overreliance for cognitive skills, and psychological and emotional dependence on chatbots. Some people have even formed romantic ties to a chatbot. Collectively, these behaviors pose risks for individuals who most need human contact.

Their constant affirmation can be limiting. Chatbots won’t engage in detrimental aggression. But human disagreements provide fodder for complex thinking and problem-solving. Challenges of communicating with people who disagree have been linked to prolonged life. AI chatbots affirm human actions even in cases where those actions are deceptive or illegal, which could cause users to take actions that harm their real-world relationships.

Finally, although nearly all our technology use consumes electricity, the AI powering today’s chatbots poses environmental impacts that we should be mindful of.

Bottom line: Chatbots serve as a beneficial “extra” in a diverse social network. But as with any technology, you must implement it effectively. Dishwashers are great for everyday plates and cups, but don't use them for the cast iron skillet.

Using a chatbot wisely can enhance your social world in new and exciting ways. But stick to what it does best.

Boyd, R. L., & Markowitz, D. M. (2026). Artificial intelligence and the psychology of human connection. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 21(2), 192–220. https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916251404394

Dagnino, F. M., Fante, C., Guerrieri, V., & Passarelli, M. (2026). Addicted, attached, or just delegating? A scoping review on “problematic artificial intelligence use”. Frontiers in Psychology, 17, Article 1900953. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900953

Folk, D., Yu, S., & Dunn, E. (2024). Can chatbots ever provide more social connection than humans? Collabra: Psychology, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.117083

#4733. Why volunteers are gluing seeds to clam shells in Connecticut

Published Oct 24, 2026 11:18 AM EDT

Environmental restoration sometimes requires out-of-the-box thinking. Along the waters of Long Island Sound in New York and Connecticut, experts are tackling the challenge of restoring crucial eelgrass habitats by gluing the plant’s seeds to clams.

Eelgrass (Zostera marina) is an important member of the ecosystem. It provides foraging areas and shelter for young fish and invertebrates, diminishes coastal erosion, draws in excess nutrients, filters water, and releases oxygen, for instance. Compared to the 1930s, eelgrass meadows in and around Long Island Sound have decreased by more than 90 percent, according to regional environmental action group Save the Sound.

To make matters worse, eelgrass is difficult to restore and there have been a lot of failed attempts, Bill Lucey, a Long Island Soundkeeper from the organization, tells Popular Science. In 2025, the team tried a different approach—recruiting clams as underwater gardeners. The strategy was originally ideated by Robert Vasiluth, the founder of Submerged Aquatic Vegetation EngineersEnvironmental (SAVE) .

The approach consists of attaching eelgrass seeds to the clam’s shells. When the clams are released into the sound, they bury into the sediment, taking the seeds down to the bottom and effectively planting them. When they conducted drone imagery to check in on their results this year, they found that the eelgrass meadow coverage had increased by 178 percent.

“It needs to survive for three years before we can really trumpet our horns and say it’s working, but the actual method of putting clams out and seeds attached to them really worked. The generation of the plants was incredible,” Lucey explains.

During their 2025 planting, the team used glue typically used in coral reef restoration to attach seeds to the clams. But then Connecticut College biologist Maria Rosa yielded better germination rates when she used wet pieces of rice paper (the kind you make spring rolls with) to seal the seeds against the shell. The Save the Sound team asked its volunteers to do the same earlier this week.

“The problem with the spring roll wrappers is yesterday [Monday, October 19], when we deployed them for the first time in scale, they weren’t all staying on,” says Lucey. “So what we’ve started doing today [Tuesday, October 20] is putting a little pocket of seeds, 10 to 20 eelgrass seeds on the top of the clam, putting a little circle of this [coral] glue around it, and then putting the spring roll wrapper stamp over that and wetting it. And so it keeps the seeds moist, and the glue holds the spring roll wrapper to the clam till it dissolves, and then it’ll release the seeds next to the clam.”

Save the Sound is aiming to release 10,000 claims and 300,000 seeds this season.

Correction: The original article misspelled Maria Rosa’s name. It has since been updated.

#4732. Tesla now says it needs its own maps for FSD after years of dismissing maps

Tesla says it’s building its own maps to fix some of the most common problems with its “Full Self-Driving” system, including reading speed limits, parking, and choosing routes. The company’s head of AI described the effort on Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call.

It’s a notable shift for a company whose CEO spent years arguing that self-driving systems relying on maps are brittle. And it shows Tesla’s fleet is now doing the same job Waymo’s cars do: mapping the roads so the self-driving system knows what it can’t reliably figure out on its own.

Tesla fans argue that Waymo’s approach differs because it creates HD maps with lidar, but ultimately both are creating their own maps; if your argument is that Tesla’s maps are less well-defined and needed for driving for different reasons than Waymo’s, you don’t really have an argument.

The question came from Tesla’s shareholder Q&A. A retail investor wrote that mapping “continues to be a problem” for FSD, listing speed limits, parking and typical routes as the three biggest issues, and asked why Tesla relies on third-party maps instead of its own.

Tesla’s VP of AI, Ashok Elluswamy, agreed that “we shouldn’t be depending on external people’s maps.” He said Tesla is building its own maps using a new AI-based mapping and navigation architecture, fed by what the fleet collectively learns, that will also learn individual drivers’ preferences and respond to voice commands.

He said the technology will start handling the beginning and end of trips with FSD v15, and over the following months take over navigation, parking and destination handling.

Tesla has gone back and forth on this before.

In 2015, when it launched Autopilot, Tesla told Fortune it had started building high-precision maps with “100 times the level of granularity” of standard navigation, using data from its customer cars.

At its Autonomy Day in 2019, Elon Musk said Tesla had tried high-precision lane maps and realized it was “a huge mistake.” He called relying on them a “really bad idea” that makes a self-driving system “extremely brittle,” in the same presentation where he called lidar a “fool’s errand.” The message was clear: Waymo needed lidar and detailed maps, and Tesla would solve driving with cameras and AI alone, anywhere.

Seven years later, Tesla is building a map layer from its own fleet to fix the things its vision system gets wrong.

To be fair to Tesla, this isn’t an HD map in the sense Musk criticized. Tesla has always used navigation maps, and building its own instead of licensing them isn’t a contradiction on its own.

But look at the problems Tesla is trying to fix. Speed limits, parking and routes are all about understanding the environment, and FSD still often fails at it, especially with speed limit signs.

Last month, a Belgian road safety group found that FSD sped in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it tested in Brussels, averaging 44 km/h, partly because the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit in most of those zones. In the US, NHTSA is weighing an investigation into claims that Tesla Robotaxis speed through active school zones, covering about 1,000 Model Y and Cybercab vehicles.

A speed limit sign is about as simple as road information gets. If an end-to-end vision system can’t reliably read and apply it, and the fix is a better map, then vision alone isn’t doing the job Tesla said it would.

That brings Tesla closer to Waymo than it would like to admit.

Waymo maps a city by driving its sensor-equipped vehicles through it before launching service, and keeps those maps updated as its fleet drives. Tesla is now describing the same idea: its cars collect what they see, and that data feeds a Tesla-built map that helps every car drive better. The main difference is that Waymo’s cars have lidar on top.

It also fits how Tesla’s Robotaxi service actually operates: city by city, inside small geofenced service areas, with Tesla handling the fleet operations. Tesla isn’t talking about centimeter-level HD maps today, but a fleet-built map that keeps getting more detailed could easily head that way.

There’s nothing wrong with using maps. Every serious self-driving program does, and a map built from millions of Tesla cars could be a real advantage. If it fixes FSD’s speed limit problems, that’s good news for everyone sharing the road with it.

Add this as another reason why unsupervised FSD will not be going out to consumer cars in Q2 of 2027. There will be more reasons forthcoming, but not for some time as the main focus will be raking in more cash for those payday goals.

What’s wrong is the years of messaging that Tesla’s approach didn’t need any of this. Musk sold FSD as a general solution that would work anywhere through vision alone, while dismissing Waymo’s maps and lidar as crutches. Now Tesla is adding the map, it already operates in geofences, and the AI still can’t reliably read a 30 km/h sign in Brussels.

Waymo built its maps and has been running a driverless service for years. Tesla is building its maps now and has pushed unsupervised FSD in customer cars to Q2 2027, and only inside its Robotaxi fleet. At what point do we admit that both companies are solving the same problem in very similar ways, and only one of them has lidar?

We are a decade into Tesla’s self-driving effort and it is doing exactly what Musk used to say doesn’t count as a “true self-driving system”: geo-fenced areas using maps.

#4730. 6 ways bats are surprisingly human

Published Oct 24, 2026 1:30 PM EDT

Bat Week officially begins today. It’s the one week where Earth’s only winged mammals get top billing. Often associated with disease, vampires, and other generally unpleasant things, bats are actually important pollinators and play critical roles in our ecosystem.

“They’re just so cool and so interesting. During first forays into bat studies, it was just one question after another,” Rachel Page, an evolutionary biologist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama, tells Popular Science. “The more I sort of scratched the surface, the more interesting it became—which is the fun part.”

One reason bats are so interesting to scientists like Page is that they are surprisingly similar to humans. Here’s how.

Sharing a meal with good company brings immense joy for us humans. For many vampire bat species (subfamily Desmodontinae), sharing food is a matter of survival. They survive exclusively on blood and can only go about two nights without a blood meal before they die. To get around this, they rely on their social networks.

“They have the equivalent of friends. Basically, if a bat comes back from a night of foraging and has not been successful, other members of that social group will share food,” Page explains. “They’ll regurgitate blood for the bat that came back hungry.”

If that donor bat has difficulty getting food later, the one recipient will often become the donor. “So there’s this very reciprocal relationship,” says Page.

According to Page, bats will have their distinctive personalities just like people. It’s present across species, but also individual bats as well.

“You have some species that are very feisty, and they’ll go out of their way to pick a fight, and then other ones that are much more passive, calm, and very gentle,” she says.

At the edge of Panama’s Soberanía National Park, tiny, fruit-eating bats will take over the roost of larger, carnivorous bats. The Seba’s short-tailed bat (Carollia perspicillata) weighs roughly the same as a strawberry. By comparison, the frog-eating, fringed-lipped bat (Trachops cirrhosus) weighs roughly as much as an apricot and twice as much as the short-tailed bat.

Page and her colleagues in Panama have witnessed fights between the two species from roosts set up throughout the forest.

“Basically, it was the male Seba’s short-tailed bat who was instigating the fight. He was coming over and was kind of boxing and threatening much larger bats with wide open mouths and lots of teeth,” Page recalls. “And he just kept at it, and then finally, this group of fringed-lipped bats left.”

Even in the thick jungles of Panama, bats can find motionless insects on leaves. Initially, scientists believed that the thick tree cover would give small insects an “acoustic camouflage” that would confuse a bat’s echolocation system. But they were wrong.

The bats can see through this acoustic camouflage by changing the angle at which they approach the still insect.

“If you approach a flat leaf at just the right angle, you can actually get an echolocation signature,” Page explains. “You can get an echolocation signal that jumps back at you, but only if you direct your echolocation call at just the right angle.”

That’s exactly what the bats were doing in order to find insects who tried to hide in leaves.

When it’s time for the babies to wean or leave the roost, mother tent-making bats (Uroderma bilobatum) will physically prod their young with their forearms.

“There is this interesting tug that you see across so many different species. For birds, when they’re ready to fledge, there’s this sort of uncertainty.”

When sick, humans and even non-human primates change their behavior. We isolate so that the disease does not spread, and will look to plants and other sources of medicine for relief. Bats appear to change their diet to less nutritious leaves. While this may sound backwards, it’s in the hope that they have medicinal properties.

In an ongoing study with a team from the Ukrainian Bat Rehabilitation Center, the Smithsonian team is looking at the bats from Barro Colorado Island in Panama.

“We have fecal samples from these bats, so we were able to see exactly what they are eating,” says Page.

In addition to changing their diets, vampire bats will self-isolate when they are sick and others will act in a way familiar to any human parent—continuing to care for our young, even when sick.

“You don’t do as many of the normal behaviors unless it’s taking care of your babies,” says Page. “And again, it’s like a human relationship. If your little kid has a fever, you’re not going to shut them in a room and leave them. You’re not going to desert them.”

To find dinner, the fringe-lipped bat (Trachops cirrhosus) will listen in on their prey’s mating calls. These frog-eating bats eavesdrop on the mating calls that the male frogs use to attract females. They then use the calls to assess if the frog is edible or poisonous before going in for the kill.

“They’ve really cracked this communication of another entire group,” says Page.

According to Page, it’s similar to being in a quiet room and hearing someone open up a bag of potato chips and is loudly eating. The noise makes everyone pay attention. “Bats attend to those acoustic signals of other bats, and that attention then helps them learn,” Page says. “They can learn those distinctions of palatable versus poisonous, and they can learn that socially as well from observing the other behaviors with bats.”

To learn more about bats and how to help protect them, visit Bat Week’s website.

#4729. BMW is already discounting the new iX5 with a $1,000 loyalty bonus

The iX5 is set to go on sale in early 2027, but BMW is already offering a loyalty discount to sweeten the deal for those looking to stay with the brand.

Following the new iX3 and i3, the iX5 will go on sale in early 2027 with BMW’s Neue Klasse-inspired design, technology, and sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system.

The iX5 is the first fully electric BMW X5. For its fifth generation, the BMW X5 will be available in gas, plug-in hybrid (PHEV), and battery electric (EV) powertrains in the US. Overseas markets will also see diesel and hydrogen fuel-cell versions.

While the gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now available, the electric iX5 still says it’s “coming in 2027” on BMW’s website.

BMW is already sweetening the deal with a $1,000 loyalty discount for returning buyers or lessees, according to a memo CarsDirect reviewed that was sent to dealers.

Although a $1,000 credit may not seem like much, it’s twice what BMW is offering for the 2027 iX3. The discount doesn’t require a trade-in and can be stacked with other offers.

BMW’s loyalty discount provides a cash rebate off the MSRP when you buy or lease a new BMW through BMW Financial Services and have owned or leased another BMW within the last 12 months.

The iX5 doesn’t have any other current discounts or lease offers, but keep an eye out closer to launch.

Earlier this week, BMW showcased the i5’s fast-charging capabilities for the first time during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic. During the event, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The iX5 60 xDrive uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW estimates will offer up to 435 miles of range.

Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric SUV delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, and can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds. It can also tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse setup, with a wide 17.9″ central touchscreen and BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the base of the windshield. Buyers can also add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen.

Measuring 197.2″ in length, 78.7″ in width, and 68.9″ in height, the iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

You have to wonder why Tesla’s name keeps coming up in this discussion, too. This BMW has a net battery capacity of 144 kWh and achieves an energy density Tesla hasn’t even come close to matching. Tesla wanted to get there, but the 4680 battery has been a technical disaster. Even the Cybertruck has a significantly smaller battery. On top of that, the BMW is highly efficient, thanks to its electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM), which doesn’t use rare earths. We’re talking about cutting-edge technology here, in a completely different league from Tesla.

BMW will officially launch the 2027 iX5 50 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800.

The iX5 is the first all-electric BMW model produced in the US. Production is set to begin at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year.

#4728. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4726. Why do dead bodies move and make noise?

Published Oct 25, 2026 7:54 AM EDT

Death is supposed to be the end of the road. The lights are out, the curtain has fallen. No breathing, no heartbeat—end of discussion, right? Not quite.

In some cases, corpses twitch, flex, shift, change positions, or even make noises that could easily be mistaken for messages from beyond the grave. But before you call the Ghostbusters, take a deep breath. The explanation is less zombie apocalypse and more basic biology.

Even after the heart stops beating, the body still has a few tricks left up its sleeve. The results can be creepy, sure, but experts say they’re perfectly natural. Here’s why corpses sometimes move and make noise.

Our bodies can continue moving long after death. When researchers in Australia used time-lapse cameras to keep tabs on a decomposing human body, they discovered that it continued to shift for at least 16 months, with some parts moving as much as 20 total inches over the course of the study period.

Researchers call this “post-mortem movement”—and it’s a lot less dramatic than you might imagine.

“A body can move, but not necessarily in the way that I think most people envision,” Derek Boyd, a biological anthropologist who co-directs the Forensic Anthropology and Bioarchaeology Laboratory at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, tells Popular Science.

“The movements are very subtle—you’re not going to see a body sit up or turn its head.”

After death, the human body moves through a pretty predictable series of decomposition stages. One of the earliest is rigor mortis, when the muscles stiffen and the body becomes rigid. As this process unfolds, a corpse may shift, creating the appearance of movement—but it’s easy to miss, Boyd says.

“You’re not necessarily going to see [the movement] unless you’re laser-focused on the body for the first 48 hours—and even then it’s just going to look like tension, just the body stiffening,” he says.

The next stages in which movement might occur are boat and post-bloat, says Boyd. When someone dies, the body’s own enzymes begin breaking down its cells, a process known as autolysis.

Meanwhile, bacteria and microbes start spreading throughout the body, digesting tissues and producing gases. This process, known as putrefaction, can “cause the body to become distended or start to bloat, and that bloating can result in a dramatic expansion,” he says. “The body inflates in various places. But, again, this is something that happens gradually.”

Eventually, those gases escape—and the body gradually deflates, sometimes causing small shifts in its position.

Finally, in the advanced stages of decomposition, the body’s soft tissues begin to dry out, a process known as desiccation. “We have ligaments that are attaching bones together, tendons connecting muscle to bone, and in these later stages of decomposition, those connective tissues can shrink and tighten—and, in doing so, they can pull on our skeleton in various ways,” he says.

Of course, not all postmortem movement comes from decomposition itself. Outside forces can also cause a body to shift or change position. Scavengers may drag or disturb remains while feeding, for example, while insects can move small body parts or contribute to the breakdown of tissues. Environmental factors, such as wind, flowing water, or shifting soil, can also displace remains over time.

While we’re alive, our bodies are constantly making noise—burps, farts, stomach gurgles, and growls, creaks, and cracks. Considering how noisy our living bodies can be, it shouldn’t come as much of a surprise that they can continue making noises after death.

As gases build up during putrefaction, for instance, the body can produce gurgles, bubbles, groans, or even noises that sound like sighs, Sarah Chavez, executive director of the Order of the Good Death, a nonprofit that aims to change how people think about death and make end-of-life care and funeral options more accessible and equitable, tells Popular Science. Fluids and gases can also get pushed through the mouth or nose, which can sometimes create surprising sounds, she says.

“It can be startling if you’re not expecting it, but there’s nothing supernatural happening,” Chavez adds. “The body is just continuing to do what bodies do—break things down, move fluids and gases around, and occasionally make unintentional noises.”

Ultimately, the fact that bodies can move or make noises after death is a reminder that the human body is “a beautiful ecosystem of its own,” says Boyd.

In life, our bodies are home to countless microorganisms that interact with one another and help keep us alive. After death, those same microorganisms continue to play a role in the body’s breakdown, creating the conditions that can cause a twitch, a shift in position, or an unexpected sound.

The body no longer has thoughts, feelings, or aspirations, but it remains a complex biological system in its own right. “We are walking ecosystems, and we remain ecosystems even after death,” says Boyd.

And scientists are still learning what these postmortem ecosystems can tell us. For example, Boyd says researchers are exploring whether changes to the body’s microbial communities could help forensic investigators estimate how much time has passed since someone died—a “microbial clock” of sorts. In other words, the very same processes that can make a corpse move or make noises may also offer valuable clues about the biology of death itself.

#4725. Seattle plans 200 curbside EV charging stations – and you can request one

Seattle plans to add up to 200 public curbside Level 2 EV charging stations by 2030, and residents can now request one near their home or apartment.

For apartment dwellers and anyone who parks on the street, that’s a useful alternative to making a separate trip to charge. More than half of Seattle’s homes are apartments or condos, according to City Light. Older houses and houseboats can also lack somewhere to plug in off the street.

Seattle City Light and the Seattle Department of Transportation are targeting neighborhoods with the fewest charging options.

The chargers are intended for topping up while parked near home. Seattle says its Level 2 curbside EV charging stations can add around 12–30 miles of range per hour, depending on the vehicle and equipment. All the new locations will be open to the public.

City Light currently charges $0.21 per kilowatt-hour at its Level 2 chargers. At that rate, adding 30 kWh would cost $6.30. Using the utility’s estimate of about 3 miles per kWh, that’s roughly 90 miles of range, depending on the EV and driving conditions.

The expansion follows a 2023–2024 pilot at 31 locations, which SDOT says drew strong use and positive community feedback. Seattle’s installations will be funded by the transportation levy voters approved in 2024.

Residents can request a curbside charger through City Light’s program page. Applications will remain open through fall 2027, with locations reviewed and selected on an ongoing basis. The city will consider charging gaps, environmental and equity goals, and whether a site has the electrical infrastructure needed for installation.

#4724. An Abandoned Pacifier Stirs a Moving Conversation

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

My friend told me about an experience that jolted her the other morning. She is my age, give or take a few years, and the mother of two adult daughters.

She was walking near the Hudson River when she spotted an upturned pacifier/dummy on the ground.

This image brought a flood of memories for her and became a visceral reminder of her own early mothering days. She told me about this, and I immediately connected with her experience. We gave ourselves the space to indulge our own imaginings and immerse ourselves in our individual inner worlds.

There is something embedded in the form of a dummy, which is intriguing. Maybe it's the shape, adapted from the maternal breast, and the meaning this can hold. Maybe it's something about the maternal collective unconscious and our need to soothe our child at any cost; our hope of harmony with our infant. The pacifier is also a gauge of social judgement; do "good mothers" use them?

My friend’s story took me back to the early days of my mothering. For me, the dummy played a prominent part in the mothering of each of my children. It represented an almost sacred object holding the potential of a peaceful retreat for my infant and myself.

A similar playbook emerged for each of my children. Each time, there was an initial resistance to the dummy, quickly followed by acceptance as my baby ceded to its comfort.

I remember the wonder of watching my baby’s rhythmic sucking, the fluttering of the eyes. Then, a momentary halt to the sucking, as if he forgot. Then, the sucking started again. I was mesmerized watching my baby remembering and forgetting, her eyes fluttering while drifting off to blissful sleep in her own world; being aware of the dummy one minute, and then unaware.

This was often followed by a release of the dummy, a realization, and a cry as it was gently returned to his mouth so the sucking could continue. This became a regular routine which brought confidence and solace. A respite for both of us.

Then, my memories shifted to that of my older infant’s cot filled with dummies one minute, then empty the next. My infant never tired of this game of throwing and retrieving it.

It has dawned on me that this game held so much meaning for my later understanding of mothering. The importance of laughter and games and the reality that the dummy, like the mother, is both necessary and dispensable over time.

Then, my thoughts began to meander back to this particular dummy left on the street. What is its story?

Is there a baby crying and screaming for it? How will the baby and the mother manage without it?

Who lost it? Maybe the father? The grandmother? Did a sibling throw it out? Was it older children or teenagers playing with it for a stunt?

Was this an infant’s planned farewell to this dummy?

Is there a mum somewhere ferreting through her diaper bag to find it, or is she looking for another, saying to herself, “Why did I only bring one?”

The anticipated and real screams from her baby, and worrying about how she would soothe her.

What about characteristics of the dummy itself? Is it pink or blue or maybe white? Is it new or old? What does this tell us about the baby?

Is it a newborn’s dummy? Is it one of those new ergonomic ones, which is a reminder of the years that have passed since my own hands-on mothering and what has changed?

Then, some truths about dummies/pacifiers:

For some women, a dummy has no meaning, and for others it means so much.

The idea of a dummy is also wrapped up in the social and inner discourse of judgment. In my day, there was a lot of narrative surrounding the use of dummies, many shoulds and should nots. Does a good mom give her baby a dummy? Is she lazy? Will it damage her baby’s bite and teeth? If you give your child one, how do you get rid of it? Will he still be walking around with it at 3 or 4 years of age?

Questions such as these return to the everlasting judgment and moral reckoning that mothers continually endure and can hopefully challenge.

My friend’s story of the dummy abandoned on the ground provokes reflection:

For the current hands-on mother, the dummy captures multiple moments, thoughts, and possibilities of her everyday life: The many challenges that are embodied in the face of an inconsolable child. The mother’s constant striving to soothe her child, to do her best, and the reality that there is a continual struggle between her own and her baby’s needs and questions about how these are balanced.

It is a reminder of the social judgment that surrounds the mother, where she really needs compassion, support, and encouragement to name and manage her daily life and her feelings. Our job as post-hands-on mothers is to champion this cause.

For mothers such as myself and my friend, while we are no longer hands-on, we own our memories. They are treasures that we forever hold that belong only to us and one day to our daughters. Moments of bliss, connection, and struggle are embodied in the image of a dummy.

The power of these objects offers a valuable and seamless conduit back to that time and into the future, embodying what we are as mothers, immortalizing our maternal memories, and continuing to enrich our lives.

Like many new BYD models, the cabin adopts a minimalist design with premium features like ambient lighting, a three-spoke steering wheel, and higher-end materials.

Ahead of its official launch, the Denza N8 EV was spotted in China undisguised. New images from Autohome show the luxury SUV driving in public, with roof-mounted LiDAR and a sleek, premium look.
